en: Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa!

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One, Vajrasattva, was dwelling in the bhaga of Vajradhātvīśvarī, the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, together with a multitude of many vajrayogins and yoginīs, such as the vajrayogin Śvetācala, the vajrayogin Pītācala, the vajrayogin Raktācala, the vajrayogin Śyāmācala, the vajrayoginī Mohavajrī, and the vajrayoginī Piśunavajrī.
Together with Rāgavajrī Vajrayoginī, Īrṣyāvajrī Vajrayoginī, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yogis and yoginīs headed by these, [he dwelt].
Then the Blessed One, Vajrasattva, having entered the meditative absorption of Kṛṣṇācala, uttered this:
"I am liberated from existence and non-existence, solely intent upon the four joys;
my nature is free from conceptual proliferation, devoid of all discursive thought."
Those fools who do not know me as abiding within the bodies of all men—
for their benefit, I am established in five forms.
Then the Blessed Lady Vajradhātvīśvarī, having entered the samādhi of Dveṣavajrī, proclaimed this:
"I am inseparable from emptiness and compassion, abiding in the bliss of divine sensual pleasure;
I am devoid of all conceptual constructions, free from proliferation, and undisturbed."
Those women who do not know me as abiding within the bodies of all women—
for their benefit, I am present in five forms.

Then the Blessed One Kṛṣṇācala, having kissed and embraced the Blessed Lady Dveṣavajrī with intensity, addressed her: "O Goddess, O Goddess! This is most delightful, a secret exceedingly difficult to obtain, the essence of essences, the most excellent, well-spoken by all the Buddhas."
Listen, I shall proclaim the supreme Great Tantra, the sovereign of the kings of tantras,
known by the name Ekalavīra, for the sake of the swift accomplishment of sentient beings.
This tantra is not to be revealed to one who has not seen a maṇḍala;
indeed, one should not show this king of tantras to one who has entered another maṇḍala.
To one who has entered the mandala of Caṇḍaroṣa with a concentrated mind,
and who is devoted to faith and diligence regarding Caṇḍa, one should indeed teach this tantra.
To one who is devoted to the guru, compassionate, dedicated to the vehicle of mantra,
and constantly devoted to Caṇḍeśvara, one should reveal this tantra.
Having understood this, any yogin who is nevertheless mocked by greed might teach this supreme tantra in a place where the mandala of Caṇḍa has not been seen.
Seized by great diseases and defiled by excrement and urine,
he will experience the suffering of death within six months.
Then, seized by the messengers of Yama and brought under the power of the noose of Time,
the sinner is led to hell, even if he were protected by the Buddhas themselves.
If, after experiencing suffering due to the exhaustion of karma for a hundred thousand years,
one attains a human birth, even that is shattered by the thunderbolt.
Therefore, the practitioner who knows the mantras and observes the vow should draw a beautiful mandala there,
having first admitted the disciples who have already been tested.
Therefore, one should teach this tantra, which is difficult to find in the three worlds;
even he who teaches what has not been heard goes to the lower realms.
Even if he were equal to a Buddha, his mouth would fester if he is devoid of faith, or if a disciple listens merely out of a desire for knowledge.
It will be split at the crown by a thunderbolt during the rainy season; of this there is no doubt.
This truth has been spoken by me, O Goddess, O lady of beautiful countenance.
And in this *Caṇḍaroṣaṇa* tantra, which is well-guarded and consists of a single hero;
Thus ends the first chapter, on the introduction to the tantra, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
[Chapter A2] Then the Blessed Lady Dveṣavajrī, firmly embracing the Blessed Lord Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, said:
"What is the measurement of the maṇḍala, and by whom should it be drawn?"
And it should be written there in the middle accordingly; tell me, O Lord, what [should be written].
Then the Blessed One said: "The measurement of the mandala should be one cubit, two cubits, three cubits, four, or five; the fifth measurement is five, and it should not exceed that."
With the powder of that very [substance], prepared in various colors,
one should [draw] a square with four gates, adorned with four archways.
One should fashion its gateway using exactly one-eighth part;
the turret (niryūha) should be equal in measure to the gateway, and the pilaster (kapolaka) half of that.
Likewise, one should [draw] the wings, the altar (vedī), the necklaces (hārā), the half-necklaces (ardhahāra), and the fillets (paṭṭikā);
outside its root-line, one should [draw] the ground for the colored powders (rajobhū) with exactly half that measure.
One should fashion a vajra-fence with that very [material], as well as eight pillars;
one should make the excellent door-arch three times the size of the door.
Having drawn a double-vajra at the bottom, surrounded by a vajra-fence and adorned with wish-fulfilling trees and other ornaments, one should depict the maṇḍala of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa.
One enclosure should be made, circular like a wheel;
upon it, one should draw eight double-lotuses starting from the east.
In the center of that [mandala], in the middle, is a ninth [deity] with a very dark blue sword marked by a vajra,
joined with a vajra-knife and a skull-cup.
In the east, one should draw a white-colored sword marked with a wheel;
in the south, however, one should draw a yellow-colored one joined with a jewel.
In the west, one should draw [the deity] red in color, marked with a red lotus;
in the north, one should draw [the deity] dark-blue in color, bearing only a sword.
One should draw a white sword marked with a wheel in the southeast corner;
one should draw a yellow-colored [sword] marked with a jewel in the southwest.
Likewise, in the northwest, she is red and marked with a red lotus;
in the northeast, she is dark-complexioned and endowed with a blue lotus.
One should fashion all the symbols situated above the moon and sun;
this is what has been taught by me as the powder mandala for accomplishing the welfare of the world.
Alternatively, one should construct a mandala well-drawn in the form of a cloth painting;
having drawn the mandala as before, one should depict Kṛṣṇācala in the center.
One should indeed draw the *Sampuṭa* of Dveṣavajrī in the east,
then white Acala on the right, and red Acala on the back.
One should draw Śyāmācala in the north; in the southeast, Mohavajrī;
and one should likewise draw white Piśunavajrī in the southwest.
In the northwest, one should paint the goddess Lohitā, Rāgavajrī;
in the northeast, one should indeed paint the dark-green Īrṣyāvajrī on the cloth mandala.
Now follows the mantra for the consecration of the maṇḍala:
Oṃ, Śrī Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, together with your entire retinue, come, come! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Perform the consecration here in this maṇḍala! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Having drawn [the deity] with this, having caused [him] to enter, having bound [him], and having brought [him] under control, one should worship.
Now follows the mantra for worship:
Oṃ kṛṣṇācala, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ śvetācala, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, yellow Acala, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, red Acala, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, dark-green Acala, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ dveṣavajri, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ mohavajri, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ piśunavajri, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ rāgavajri, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ īrṣyāvajri, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ!
One should indeed perform the worship of the maṇḍala with the five offerings: flowers, lamps, incense, perfumes, and food.
When Śvetācala is in the center, accompanied by Mohavajrī, his very mandala is to be known; likewise for Pītācala and the others.
One who has exerted effort in the preliminary service should, with a one-pointed mind, perform the visualization of the five maṇḍalas according to the fivefold division of yogins.
Having surrounded the mandala, one should feed the yoginī who is embraced by the yogi with wine and meat, and one should pay homage to her again and again.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Maṇḍala Chapter, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekallavīra.
[Chapter A3] Then the Blessed One said: "How may a disciple become worthy and fit to be engaged in this tantra?"
And you should act without hesitation; speak, O Great Lord!
Then the Blessed One said: "First one should grant the three refuges, the five precepts, and the poṣadha;
thereafter, the five empowerments, followed by the secret, the wisdom, and finally the remaining [empowerment]."
Then one becomes a worthy disciple; to him alone should one teach the tantra.
One should avoid another from afar; otherwise, one will go to the Raurava hell.
In this regard, there is this verse on the three refuges:
"I go for refuge to the Buddha until I reach the seat of enlightenment;
I go for refuge to the Dharma and to the Saṅgha with unwavering faith."
In this regard, there is this verse on the five precepts:
I renounce killing, theft, another’s wife, false speech, And fifthly, intoxicants— renouncing them all like a snake.
In this regard, the Uposatha verse is as follows:
"I shall not kill a living being; I shall not take what belongs to another;
I shall practice celibacy; and I shall avoid false speech."
I shall never drink intoxicants, the source of heedlessness;
I shall also avoid dancing, singing, ornaments, and festive celebrations.
High beds, grand couches, and eating at improper times—
one should thus train in accordance with the Arhats in the eightfold Poṣadha.
I shall maintain this pure [teaching] exactly as taught by the Buddha;
thereby, having conquered the deceitful Māra and attained supreme Buddhahood, [I shall bring benefit to all beings].
May I become a refuge for all embodied beings weary of existence;
may I remain as a person born of the Sugata throughout the duration of cyclic existence.
May I associate with the virtuous, be wise, and be devoted to the welfare of the world.
In this regard, this is the water consecration:

having visualized the disciple as pure, resembling crystal, and stainless, one should draw water from the *vijaya* flask with a mango sprout and consecrate him with the mantra: *Oṃ āḥ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye hūṃ*.

In this regard, this is the crown consecration (*makuṭābhiṣeka*). Having fashioned a crown from cloth and other materials and considering it to be like all the jewels, and having visualized the disciple as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), one should place the crown upon his head and consecrate him as before: *oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa āviśa āviśa asya hṛdaye hūṃ phaṭ*.
In that regard, this is the sword consecration (*khaḍgābhiṣeka*):
having placed a sword made of iron or other materials into his right hand, one should consecrate him as before with the mantra: *oṃ hana hana māraya māraya sarvaśatrūñ jñānakhaḍga hūṃ phaṭ*.

In this regard, this is the initiation of the noose (*pāśābhiṣeka*). Having placed a noose made of copper or other materials into the left hand joined with the index finger, one should perform the initiation as before: *oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa kaṭṭa kaṭṭa sarvaduṣṭān pāśena bandha bandha mahāsatya te dharma te svāhā*.
In this regard, this is the name-consecration (*nāmābhiṣeka*).

Having seated the disciple with the mudrā of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa and having focused upon him in that form, [the preceptor says]: *Oṃ he śrībhagavan kṛṣṇācala siddhas tvaṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Then one should consecrate him as before. In this way, the consecration by the names of the five immovable ones (*pañcācala*) according to the distinctions of the colors, such as black and so forth, should be given to the practitioner. Thus is the fivefold consecration.

For women, however, one should omit the *makuṭābhiṣeka* (crown-consecration) and instead bestow the *sindūrābhiṣeka* (vermilion-consecration). Taking hold of the disciple, who has the form of the Great Goddess Paṭu, [the master should say]: *Oṃ bhagavati āviśa āviśa asyā hṛdaye hūṃ phaṭ*. He should place a knife made of iron or other metal into her right hand, saying: *Oṃ karttike sarvamārāṇāṃ māṃsaṃ kartaya kartaya hūṃ phaṭ*. Into her left hand he should give a human skull-cup (*kapāla*) made of wood or similar material, saying: *Oṃ kapāla sarvaśatrūṇāṃ raktaṃ dhāraya dhāraya hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, having seated her with the Bhagavatī-mudrā and having taken hold of her in that form, one should consecrate women by means of the names of the five yoginīs according to their distinctions of color, such as black and so forth, [with the mantra]: *Oṃ he śrīdveṣavajri siddhā tvaṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. For these [women], however, the empowerment of skillful means (*upāyābhiṣeka*) is to be given in place of the wisdom empowerment (*prajñābhiṣeka*).
Now follows the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*).
Having honored the guru with garments and other offerings, the disciple should present to him a woman adorned with beauty and youth, who is desired by his own mind.
"This [woman], who bestows all the pleasures of desire, is offered to you."
For the sake of sensual pleasure, take me, O Lord; have mercy!

Then, having prostrated to the guru, the disciple should go outside and remain there while reciting the mantra: *Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ*. The guru, moreover, having honored himself with liquor, meat, and so forth, and having gratified the Prajñā, should enter into union (*sampuṭībhūya*). Having placed the resulting semen and blood in a leaf-cup or similar vessel, he should summon the disciple; then, taking the substance with his ring finger and thumb upon the disciple’s tongue, he should write the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.

Then one should recite, "Ah, what happiness! and then speak as follows: "Today I generate that Buddha-knowledge by which the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present have attained non-abiding nirvāṇa. However, you must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala; if you do speak of it, then [the following shall happen]."
Having placed the sword upon the heart of that disciple, one should recite this:
"For this sword is exceedingly sharp, held in the hand of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa;
it is intent upon cutting whoever would violate the samaya."
Throughout thousands of millions of births, men with swords held in their hands become those who sever all limbs, intent solely upon decapitation.
"It shall be so for you as well, if you break this agreement.
Then the disciple should say, "So be it."

Then, having bound a blindfold, one should have the disciple cast a flower upon the maṇḍala. Then, having removed the blindfold, one should show the maṇḍala and explain which [deity] corresponds to whichever mark [the flower fell upon]. Thereafter, one should entrust that very Prajñā to the disciple.
This delightful dhāraṇī, revealed by the Buddhas, is to be cultivated;
the fool who transgresses it shall not attain supreme accomplishment.

Then the Guru should explain the division of the four joys into the ear. Then the Guru should go outside; the Prajñā, having become naked, shows her secret organ while squatting, pointing with her index finger.
"Are you able, my child, to consume my impurities—
the drinking of feces, urine, blood, and what is within the womb?"
The practitioner should say:
"O Mother, how could I not venture to consume your impurity?
I must cultivate devotion toward women until I reach the seat of enlightenment."
And she said:
"O, for him who would serve my lotus, which is endowed with all happiness,
according to the prescribed rite, I shall be the bestower of accomplishment."
O Padmā, act as is required; maintain fortitude through the application of fortitude, for Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa himself abides here in great bliss.

Then the practitioner, having meditated upon himself in the form of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa and having formed a union with the Wisdom Consort (prajñā) in the form of Dveṣavajrī, should perceive the four joys (caturānanda). Then, once that is accomplished, he should perform the gaṇacakra with wine, meat, and so forth, placing the Guru at its head. This is the Wisdom Empowerment (prajñābhiṣeka).
Thus ends the third chapter, on consecration, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
[Chapter A4] Then the Blessed One said:
"How indeed should one who is a practitioner of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa perform the meditation?"
O Supreme Lord, tell me what kind of mantra is to be recited.
Then the Blessed One said:
"In a place agreeable to the mind and free from all disturbances,
one who is composed should prepare a seat there, using whatever is available."
One should first cultivate loving-kindness; in the second [moment], one should meditate on compassion;
in the third, one should cultivate sympathetic joy; and finally, one should cultivate equanimity toward all.
Then, one should visualize the seed-syllable situated upon a lotus, moon, and sun within the heart;
by means of its rays, one should meditate on Caṇḍaroṣaṇa as fully manifested before oneself.
The wise one should mentally worship him with flowers, incense, and other offerings;
in his presence, he should confess his sins and rejoice in all merit.
One should go for refuge to the Three Jewels, as well as offer prayers and requests;
then, having surrendered oneself, one should dedicate the merit.
Then, having made an aspiration, one should direct the mind toward enlightenment;
thereafter, one should perform prostrations and again withdraw [the visualization] with rays of light.
Having recited this mantra, one should indeed practice the meditation on emptiness.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
One should diligently contemplate that the syllable *hūṃ* is consumed by rays of light;
having meditated on it like the burning of camphor, one should not even conceptualize the rays.
Having meditated for a mere moment on everything as being like space,
one should visualize one's own body as clear as pure crystal.
One should first meditate upon the four syllables Yaṃ, Raṃ, Vaṃ, and Laṃ;
having visualized them as perfected, one should thereby [visualize] the elements of wind, fire, water, and earth.
Then, having meditated upon the syllable *Bhṛṃ*, one should fashion a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*),
which is square, possesses four doors, and is adorned with eight pillars.
One should meditate upon a universal lotus with eight petals in its center,
produced from the seed-syllable *paṃ*, and within that, the moon born from the syllable *aṃ*.
One should meditate on the sun arising from the syllable *raṃ*, and above that, again the syllable *hūṃ*;
from that, one should visualize Akṣobhya in union with Māmakī.
There, the lord of yogins should transfer [the consciousness] through the aperture at the crown of his head,
by means of the yoga of Tārā’s transference and with a mind focused on Māmakī’s bhaga.
Then, having become semen and fluid, it falls into the womb of her vulva;
once fully formed, it emerges from the vulva in a fierce form.
One should slay Akṣobhya with a sword and afterwards devour the father;
then one should likewise imagine Māmakī as having been devoured by him.
Then, having taken my mother Māmakī, one should desire her;
one should meditate on oneself embraced by her in the form of Dveṣavajrī.
Holding a fierce sword in his right hand and a noose in his left,
he threatens with his index finger, his fangs pressed against his lip.
The posture of combat is with the right leg trampling the four Māras, while the left knee rests upon the ground; he has squinting eyes and is terrifying.
He threatens the earth with his left knee placed forward;
he has Akṣobhya as his crown and is blue in color, wearing a jeweled diadem.
And the youth Pañcacīra, adorned with all ornaments,
appearing as one sixteen years of age, the Lord with two red eyes.
One should meditate with a steady mind: "I am the perfected Caṇḍaroṣaṇa.
Then, by means of the churning yoga, one should first create White Acala.
One should emanate Mohavajrī in the southeast, with a radiance like the autumnal *puṇḍarīka* lotus;
one should emanate Piśunavajrī in the southwest, and yellow Acala in the south.
One should emanate Raktācala behind [the central deity], and Rāgavajrikā, who is red;
Śyāmācala and Śyāmā in the northwest and the north, respectively, and [Śvetācala and Śvetā] in the northeast.
Thereafter, he should emanate Īrṣyāvajrī, who brings about the arising of wisdom;
then the goddesses urge him on with songs arising from their own throats.
O Lord, may you remain free from attachment; do not become one whose nature is void.
For even in separation, all things will eventually fall away, as indeed they all must.
O Vajra of Delusion!
Do not be cruel; O Lord, do not become empty.
Do not abandon me, for I am deeply afflicted; otherwise, this soul will become destitute.
O Piśunavajrī, may they be joyful; you have made them enter into emptiness.
Now, having offered the invitation, the human being remains with only a trace of attachment.
O Rāgavajrī,
disregarding the attainment of youth, which is fruitless and empty, and having abandoned that empty nature, establish your resolve upon me alone.
Free from envy,
having heard this as if in a dream, he rose up immediately and swiftly;
he should meditate upon him in his former form, consisting of the *sampuṭa*.
Then, having slain Śvetācala, one should desire Mohavajrī;
having assumed the form of Śvetācala, one should again slay Pītācala.
One should desire Piśunavajrī, having made her of the nature of yellow Acala;
likewise, having slain red Acala, one should desire Rāgavajrikā.
Having assumed the nature of Rakta-acala, one should then strike Śyāmācala;
thereafter, having assumed the nature of Śyāmācala, one should perform the rite for the sake of desire by means of Īrṣyāvajrī.
Having gratified the four goddesses, he should dissolve the entire mandala;
the ascetic should then intensely contemplate himself as a single, unified whole.
Then one should cultivate the ego-sense: "I am indeed accomplished," without any doubt. For that yogi who is black in color is a devotee of Kṛṣṇācala.
For the yogi who is white-complexioned is a meditator on Śvetācala;
the yogi who is yellow-colored is a meditator on Pītācala.
For that yogi who is red and white is a meditator on Raktācala;
for that yogi who is dark-complexioned is a meditator on Śyāmācala.
A woman who is black in color should visualize herself as Dveṣavajrī;
a woman who is white and fair should visualize herself as Mohavajrī.
A woman who is yellow in color should visualize herself as Piśunavajrī;
a woman who is reddish-white should visualize herself as Rāgavajrī.
A woman who is dark-complexioned should visualize herself as Īrṣyāvajrī;
every man is a Vajrayogin, and every woman is a Vajrayoginī.
One should conceive of all this through the distinction of colors, such as black and so forth;
or alternatively, there is a fivefold conceptualization according to the distinction of ritual actions.
For Kṛṣṇa is for killing and hatred; Śveta for pacification and likewise for thought;
Pīta for paralyzing and nourishing; and Lohita for subjugation and attraction.
The dark-complexioned is renowned for expulsion (*uccāṭana*), or else according to the distinction of caste:
the black is a *ḍomba*, the white is a Brahmin, and the yellow is considered a *caṇḍāla*.
The actor is red, while the washerman is remembered as dark;
one whose disposition is dark should desire a large-eyed girl of dark complexion.
One who is white-souled [unites] with a white maiden, while one who is very yellow [unites] with a yellow maiden;
indeed, a red man [unites] with a red maiden, and a dark man with a dark maiden.
Or else, having taken whichever [form] it may be,
one intent on meditation should desire her with a steady mind, so that no one at all perceives it.
These maidens grant excellent accomplishments through practice for only a fortnight;
their semen becomes a vajra, with which one may write everything with the tongue.
Having placed his face in their vulva, he may drink their urine as much as he desires;
and having placed it in the lotus of the anus, he may indeed consume their excrement as much as he desires.
Not even the slightest aversion should be felt; otherwise, there will be a fall from accomplishment.
This is one's own excellent food, consumed by all the Buddhas.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the deities, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
Chapter A5:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the compendium of all mantras. Then the Blessed One, having entered the meditative absorption named "Victory over All Māras," spoke this compendium of mantras:
Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ. This is the root mantra.
Oṃ acala hūṃ phaṭ. This is the second root mantra.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the third root mantra.
Hūṃ | This is the heart mantra.
Āṃ. This is the second, the heart mantra.
Haṃ. This is the third heart mantra.

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ! O you of fierce form! Caṭa caṭa! Pracaṭa pracaṭa! Kaṭṭa kaṭṭa! Prasphura prasphura! Prasphāraya prasphāraya! Hana hana! Grasa grasa! Bandha bandha! Jambhaya jambhaya! Stambhaya stambhaya! Mohaya mohaya! Bind the mouths of all enemies! Trāsaya trāsaya! Mara mara! Māraya māraya! Rurucaṇḍaruk! Protect! Protect!
"Protect Devadatta! Caṇḍamahāsena commands everything. Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ. This is the garland mantra (mālāmantra)."

Homage to all the Tathāgatas, who fulfill all hopes! Sarvatācalakānanā naṭṭa naṭṭa moṭṭa moṭṭa saṭṭa saṭṭa tuṭṭa tuṭṭa tiṣṭha tiṣṭha āviśa āviśa āḥ! O great intoxicated youth, shake, shake! tiṇa tiṇa! Eat, eat the obstacles! Slay, slay the wicked! Devour, devour Devadatta! Kuru kuru kiri kiri! Great poison, vajra phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Trivalita raṅgāgartaka hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ!

Acala ceṭa phaṭ! Sphāṭaya sphāṭaya hūṃ hūṃ! Asamantika trāṭ! Mahābala sāṭaya samānaya trāṃ māṃ hāṃ! May the worlds be purified! May the Vajrin be pleased! Homage be to those of unimpeded power! Jvālaya trāṭ asaha namaḥ svāhā! This is the second garland mantra.

Homage to all the Tathāgatas who fulfill all hopes! In every way: *trāṭ*! O Amogha-caṇḍa-mahā-roṣaṇa, shatter, shatter! *hūṃ*! Cause to whirl, cause to whirl! *hūṃ*! *trāṭ*! *hāṃ*! *māṃ*! This is the third garland-mantra.
Thus are the general mantras of the five mountains.
The specific mantras are:
Oṃ kṛṣṇācala hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ Śvetācala hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ pītācala hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ Raktācala Hūṃ Phaṭ!
Oṃ Śyāmācala hūṃ phaṭ!
The general mantras of the goddesses are as follows:
Oṃ vajrayoginī hūṃ phaṭ. This is the root mantra.
Oṃ prajñāpāramite hūṃ phaṭ. This is the second root mantra.
Oṃ vauheri hūṃ phaṭ. This is the third root mantra.
Oṃ picu picu, increaser of wisdom! Jvala jvala, increaser of intelligence! Dhiri dhiri, increaser of intellect! Svāhā! This is the garland mantra (mālāmantra).
The specific mantras are as follows:
Oṃ dveṣavajri hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ mohavajri hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ piśunavajri hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ rāgavajri hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ, you who possess the vajra against envy, hūṃ phaṭ!

This is the general mantra for the *bali* offering: Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the glorious Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, who terrifies gods, asuras, and humans; who destroys the entire force of the Māras; whose head is adorned with a jeweled crown: accept, accept this *bali*; strike, strike all my obstacles; ward off, ward off the four Māras; frighten, frighten! Bewilder, bewilder! Cut, cut! Pierce, pierce! Destroy, destroy! Scorch, scorch! Dry up, dry up! Sever, sever! Split, split! The wicked beings who harbor hostile intentions toward me!
Reduce to ashes, reduce to ashes, phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Chapter on Mantras, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekallavīra.
Chapter A6:
Then the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, having firmly embraced the Blessed One and performed the friction of the lotus against the vajra, said:
"What would the cultivation be like through the yoga of the completion stage?"
For the benefit of the yoginīs, make fruitful that which has been asked.
Then the Blessed One said:
"The yogi established in the yoga of the completion stage, intent solely upon yoga,
should meditate on my form with a one-pointed mind day and night."
One should imagine one's own wife as being completely filled with your form,
so that through intense and extreme union she reaches a state of complete arousal.
One's mother, daughter, sister, niece,
and all other female relatives, as well as a *ḍombinī* and likewise a *brāhmaṇī*.
A Caṇḍālī, a Naṭakī, a Rajakī, a Rūpajīvikā,
a Vratinī, a Yoginī, and likewise a Kāpālinī;
Or one may, according to the prescribed method, enjoy another woman who is well-formed and possesses the female form as it is naturally attained, so that no breach of secrecy occurs.
But if there is a breach, Caṇḍaroṣaṇa becomes enraged and slays the practitioner;
terrifying him with his sword and noose, he casts him into the Avīci hell.
In this world there would be no success, nor likewise in the next world;
therefore, it must be kept strictly secret and not made public.
The sādhana of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa, which must be kept secret like the mantra of a ḍākinī,
was spoken by me, the Buddha, for the sake of those with extreme desire.
Having taken her— who is pleasing to his own heart and desired— into a secluded place that is agreeable to the mind and free from all disturbances.
"I am the Buddha, immovable and perfected; Prajñāpāramitā is my beloved.
Thus the wise one should meditate upon his own true nature with a deeply concentrated mind.
Having made the hermitage solitary and possessing whatever food and materials are obtained,
one should meditate intensely through the union of the two in mutual pairing.
Having brought the woman before his eyes and seated her face-to-face,
he should gaze deeply at one another with both of them out of mutual passion.
Then, meditating on the bliss of the vision, he should remain with a one-pointed mind;
by her, right there, words that produce the intensity of bliss should be spoken.
"You are my son, you are my husband; you are considered by me as brother and father. I am your mother, your wife, your sister, and your niece."
"By seven men you were my slave, my laborer, and my servant;
you were bought by me for a cowrie-shell, and I am considered your mistress."
He should fall prostrate at her feet with his hands joined in reverence,
and there he should speak these words, which are supremely conducive to happiness and the kindling of spiritual energy.
You are my mother, you are my father’s wife, and you are my niece; you are the wife of my sister’s son, you are my sister, and you are my own.
I am your servant in every way, devoted with intense bhakti;
O Mother, look upon me with compassion through the glances of your affectionate gaze.
Then, having embraced and kissed the man again and again,
she places the three-syllable mantra upon his head and the honey of her mouth’s essence into his mouth.
One should cause her to suck the lotus and display the rolling of her eyes;
having applied ointment to her mouth, one should press her heart with the breast.
Having seen his face directly before him and having placed a fingernail in its proper place, one should speak these words to him: "Eat my Vairocana!"
"Drink the water of Akṣobhya, my son; together with your father, become a servant.
I am your mistress, and your mother is also of royal lineage."
Go, my child, constantly to my feet for refuge,
since you have attained this priceless state having been nurtured by me.
Be grateful, O child; grant me the bliss born of the vajra.
Behold the three-petaled lotus, adorned with filaments in its center.
Oh, how wonderful is the field of Sukhāvatī, adorned by the Buddha Amitābha!
It bestows happiness upon those possessed of passion, peaceful, and free from all conceptual constructions.
Having cast me down supine, my mind overwhelmed by passion,
place both your feet upon my shoulders and gaze at me from below.
Then, insert the vibrating vajra into the central aperture of the lotus;
bestow upon it a thousand, ten million, or even a hundred million drops.
In my own three-petaled lotus, provided with a wick of flesh,
insert your vajra there and worship the mind with blisses.
O Vāyu, O Vāyu, [grant] to me the supreme essence of essences,
the perfectly awakened one, red like the bandhūka flower, at the tip of the vajra.
Meditating on her as she speaks thus, becoming motionless with a one-pointed mind,
he should cultivate the bliss born from that [union], remaining steady through intense concentration.
He should give her this reply: "Wait a moment, my dear, while I contemplate for just a brief instant the form residing within this woman's body."
Those talkative ones established in sinful deeds who, out of malice, revile here that one woman— the auspicious Mother of the three worlds who bestows true happiness— [suffer the consequences].
Constantly suffering in that very same fierce and unfathomable hell,
they remain for three eons, crying out with their bodies scorched by many fires.
However, it should be said that the virtue of women is their embracing of all living beings;
whether it be compassion or protection, it is firmly established in the hearts of women.
Let alone her own kin, she sustains even strangers through begging;
if she is of such a nature and not otherwise, she is a Vajrayoginī.
Let alone seeing her, or even touching or being touched by her from afar;
by the mere remembrance of her, bliss is obtained at that very moment.
The five sense objects themselves exist for women in divine forms; having married them, human beings enjoy happiness.
Therefore, O Mother, who are free from faults, adorned with all excellent qualities,
meritorious, most meritorious, and supremely auspicious, grant me your grace!
Then, seeing her tightly embraced, the yogi should press his own lip with his tooth while making a whistling sound (*sītkāra*); he should also cause her to become naked.
One should perform the Sukhodaya bind, the Dolācālana bind,
the Jānugraha bind, and also the Ūrumardana bind.
The foot-shaking bond, the earth-pressing bond,
the even-teethed bond, and the one known as the variegated bond.
The Bhramarī-jāla-bandha, the Yantrārūḍha-ūrdhvapadaka,
likewise the Kūrma-bandha, and also the Sarvatobhadra.
There, in the middle of the cross-legged posture, one should place a woman in a squatting position and join her pair of arms firmly to one's own shoulders.
Having drawn his own pair of arms out from between her armpits and inserted the vajra into the lotus, this is known as the "Arising of Bliss" (Sukhodaya) union.
The two hands joined together in a braid, one should slightly move them both; this is known as the *dolācālana* (swinging) gesture.
Placing her two knees together against one's own heart and performing the hand-placement for swaying the swing— this is the *jānukagraha* bond.
One should place her two soles against the base of one's own thighs;
because this placement brings about the arising of pleasure, this bond is called *corumardana*.
Placing the hands on her soles, navel, heart, and both sides,
this is the *pādacālana* (foot-shaking) bond produced by the movement of the swing.
Having placed her two buttocks upon the ground within the hollow of his chest,
this bond, which brings about the arising of bliss through the application [of the hands], is called *bhūmicāpita*.
Having established her in the squatting posture (utkuṭuka), one should extend both legs;
this is known as the Samadantaka bond, and one should also extend each leg individually.
Having placed her pair of feet upon his face, he should apply them to the left;
likewise on the right and in front, and then he should touch her back with his heart.
One should perform a massage of the hands and so forth; this is the binding known as Citra.
Having again brought about the arising of pleasure, one should cause her to lie on her back.
With his left hand, he should place a vajra upon her lotus;
grasping the base of her knee, he should direct it upward toward her elbow.
When their hands are interlaced like braids, it is known as the *bhramarī-jāla*;
having placed her pair of feet heavily upon one's own shoulders.
For this bond, mounted on the machine, is performed through the application of entering and entering-in;
her left foot is placed upon his shoulder, and her right [foot] at the root of her left thigh.
Placing her left foot upon his shoulder and her right foot at the root of his left thigh—
this indeed is the *ūrdhvapāda* posture, which is supremely blissful and destroys all suffering.
One should place the soles of her feet evenly against the middle of one's chest;
pressing the knees with both arms is declared to be the *kūrma-bandha* (tortoise-bind).
One should apply [the mantra] to her soles, eyes, ears, and head;
this binding is called Sarvatobhadra, which bestows all desires and happiness.
One should perform everything in a variegated manner, up to the edge of the painting;
one should press firmly with the chest through the application of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa.
And he should kiss her face again and again as much as he desires,
lifting up her face and looking at her while speaking whatever words he pleases.
One should suck her tongue and drink the saliva produced from her mouth;
one should eat the dental plaque smeared upon it and contemplate bliss.
One should slightly press the teeth and tongue against the lower lip;
with the tongue, one should cleanse the nostril openings and the corners of the eyes.
One should consume the filth produced from the teeth and the armpits, as well as everything else:
the brain, the eyes, the throat, the ears, the sides, the armpits, the hands, and the breasts.
Having kissed her, one should apply the fingernails, avoiding the two eyes;
then one should rub the *cuñca* with the hand, suck it, and thereafter bite it.
Having turned her belly upward herself, he should kiss that beautiful abdomen, repeatedly and again and again recollecting: "It was here that I dwelt before."
Touching the lotus with his hand while saying, "O Vāyu,
this is beautiful," he should give a kiss there and look [at her] after drawing it away with his hand.
Having smelled her scent, one should cleanse that opening with the tongue, thinking:
"Just as I entered through this [opening], so too have I emerged from it many times."
In that regard, one should speak these words: "This is the path of the nasal cord;
this alone shall be the path of the sixfold course through the application of ignorance."
Through the application of knowledge, however, the accomplishment of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa occurs;
then, by means of the sounds "su-kha-sī-t," there arises sweat or blood located in the lotus.
And he should eat from her mouth, gazing at it again and again;
placing his nails upon her thighs, he should massage her feet like a servant.
One should place the three-syllable [mudrā] on the head and the "small-fist" (laghumuṣṭika) in the center of the heart;
thereafter, the concentrated yogi should perform other various bindings.
There, with a mind focused solely on bliss, one should meditate upon the meditator according to one's desire;
whether he emits [semen] as desired or does not emit it, his mind remains fixed on bliss alone.
When it has been emitted, one should lick the lotus by means of kneeling down;
one should consume with the tongue the semen and blood residing within the lotus.
One should drink through the nose by means of a tube for the sake of increasing capacity;
having cleansed the lotus with the tongue, one should arouse wisdom and kiss it.
Thereafter, having embraced her, he should eat fish and meat;
he may drink milk or wine again for the sake of increasing passion.
Having exhausted their fatigue thereafter, they may then desire pleasure and the like;
then, once again, in the very same sequence as before, they should engage in mutual union.
Through this yoga of practice, the knower of yoga attains great bliss and assumes the state of Caṇḍaroṣa in this very life.
For the sake of granting accomplishment to those possessed of passion, I have revealed this yoga:
having placed the right leg playfully upon the left calf.
This celebrated sattvaparyaṅka posture bestows all desires and happiness;
it is formed by placing the left leg gracefully upon the right thigh.
This renowned lotus posture (padmaparyaṅka) bestows all desires and happiness;
having assumed the lotus posture, one should place the left leg above.
The vajraparyaṅka posture is defined as resting the left leg playfully upon the ground with the soles of the feet placed together, level and facing forward.
This squatting posture (utkuṭukāsana) should be known as the bestower of all desires;
it is performed by placing the soles of the feet on the ground, with the knees bent and spread wide apart.
This is to be known as the half-moon posture (ardhacandrāsana), which bestows the pleasure of desire;
here, the pair of knees are placed on the ground transversely, while the topknot is positioned between the two ankles.
Having performed this bow posture (*dhanvāsana*), which bestows divine sensual pleasure,
one should arrange the body into the lotus (*padma*), the thunderbolt (*vajra*), or the cross-legged (*paryaṅka*) postures.
The *utkūṭuka* and the *ardhacandra* are considered this *dhanva* posture;
having placed the woman seated in the *ardhacandrāsana* in close proximity.
Having fallen [into the mouth], one should lick the lotus while grasping the well-marked three syllables;
then, having assumed the bow posture (dhanvāsana), one places one's own face within that anus.
Having caused her anus to fall away, one should lick it as well as her nose;
through the yoga of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa, one should meditate upon the bliss arising from that.
Then the yogi shall become liberated, free from all conceptual constructions;
having made the mind devoid of passion, he should desire the Mother.
Merit is obtained through attachment, and demerit is obtained through detachment;
there is no sin greater than detachment, nor is there any merit greater than happiness.
And therefore, one should make the mind concentrated upon the happiness born of desire.

Then the Blessed Lady, her heart filled with joy, paid homage to and prostrated before the Blessed One, and spoke thus: "O Blessed One, is this method of accomplishment intended for humans alone, or for others as well?"
The Blessed One said:
"Those who are devoted here, established in all directions—
whether gods, asuras, humans, or nāgas— even they, as practitioners, shall attain accomplishment."

Then, having heard this, Maheśvara and the other gods took Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Śacī, Rati, and the other goddesses and began to meditate upon them. At that very moment—within that instant and that brief duration—all of them attained the state of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa and wandered upon the surface of the earth. There, Maheśvara was perfected as Vajraśaṅkara; Vāsudeva as Vajranārāyaṇa; Devendra as Vajrapāṇi; and Kāmadeva as Vajrānaṅga.
In this manner, the sons of the gods, headed by these, were perfected in numbers equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
Endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, acting for the benefit of all sentient beings,
and assuming various forms, all the Victors are beings who manifest through illusion.
Just as a lotus born from the mud is not defiled by the faults of the mud,
so too those born from the way of passion are not defiled by faults.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Chapter on Perfected Yoga, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
Chapter A7:
Then the Blessed One said: "For a living being engaged in sexual intercourse, there would be great exhaustion."
O Lord, you should explain his resting for the sake of sentient beings.
The Blessed One said:
Having taken hold of the bliss of the female form, which has been ceased within one's own direct perception,
one should eat fish and meat and drink liquor while remaining composed.
Whatever other food is obtained, such as cooked rice, milk, or water, one should first give it to women; only what remains after that should one consume.
When her leaf has been discarded, one should eat continuously;
and for her, one should drink water for rinsing the mouth and water used for washing the lotus.
Having taken water for the cleansing of the anus, the observer of the vow should wash his mouth and other parts;
he should consume the vomit of that woman, and he should also consume the four-fold compound (catuḥsama).
One should drink water born from the womb and eat morsels of spittle;
just as a tree, having encountered manure, becomes abundant in fruit.
In the same way, by means of the portion of impurity, a human being possesses the fruit of happiness;
for that embodied one, there is neither old age, nor disease, nor death.
He who serves even that which is impure succeeds, even if he is devoid of yoga;
whether it be edible or inedible, he should not discriminate in any way whatsoever.

The knower of Yoga does not conceptualize what is to be done and what is not to be done, nor what is approachable and what is unapproachable; he likewise does not conceive of merit or sin, nor of heaven or liberation.
The yogi, concentrated in samādhi, should remain as the single embodiment of innate bliss;
thus, if the yogi is united with yoga, he should be intent upon meditative cultivation.
By means of the singular yoga of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa,
one who maintains that ego-sense is not tainted by sins even if he should kill a hundred Brahmins.
Therefore, one should meditate upon such a protector, Caṇḍaroṣaṇa,
by whom living beings go to hell through their fierce karma.
By that very same means, however, they attain liberation without a doubt;
for it is held that all sin and merit are preceded by the mind.

Just as poison that has not been consecrated with mantras causes the destruction of life when consumed— being of a conceptual nature in the mind and differentiated by its movement, location, and so forth— [so too is the case for the mind].
By performing that very same consecration, happiness and longevity increase.
Then, at that moment, the supreme goddess Prajñāpāramitā appeared.
With a skull-bowl held in her hand, and displaying the mudrā of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa,
the greatly enraged Vajracaṇḍī should speak this supreme [mantra].
Having meditated upon my form and conceived the supreme ego-identity,
even if she were to kill a hundred Brahmins, she would not be tainted by sins.
Assuming my form with a mind solely intent on great wrath,
the yoginī may kill fish and birds, yet she is not defiled.
Women are generally merciless, fickle, angry, intent on killing, and preoccupied with wealth; it was for their sake that this [work] was revealed.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the Satisfying of the Body, in the glorious Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Tantra known as the Ekallavīra.
Chapter A8.
Then the Blessed One, having prostrated to the Blessed Lady with the five-pointed salutation, said:
"O Dear One, how indeed is your form to be known by the yogin?"
And by which yogi will the Blessed Lady be propitiated?
Then the Blessed One said:
"Whatever female form is seen in the world throughout the three realms, that is my own form appearing in low and even lower castes."
A goddess, an asura woman, a yakṣiṇī, and likewise a rākṣasī;
a nāginī, a daughter of a bhūtinī, a kinnarī, and likewise a human woman.
A Gandharvī, a Nārakī, a Tiryakkanyā, and a Pretikā;
a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriṇī, a Vaiśyā, and a Śūdrī—these are of extreme variety.
The daughter of a scribe, the princess, the female supervisor,
the female handmaid, the merchant’s wife, the water-carrier, the courtesan, the boatwoman, and the leather-worker.
The woman of the Kula, the woman of the Triṇa, the Ḍombī, the Caṇḍālī, and likewise the Śavarī;
the washerwoman, the vintress, the woman of the perfumed water, and the woman of action.
The barber’s wife, the actress, the brazier, the goldsmith, the fisherwoman, the basket-maker, the potter, and also the garland-maker.
Kāpālinī, Śaṅkhinī, Varuḍinī, Kemālinī, Gopālī, Kāṇḍakārī, Kocinī, and Śilākuṭī.
The mother-in-law, the female barber, and those encompassed by all castes;
the mother, the sister, the wife, and my own niece.
The younger sister, the own sister, and any woman of all castes;
the female ascetic, the female yoginī, the widow, and even the female practitioner of austerities.
Thus, all these many women, united with my form,
abide for the sake of all sentient beings, established as certain in their own respective natures.
By means of kisses, embraces, and so forth, according to their availability,
these very [women] become served by yogins through the union of the vajra and the lotus.
When served, women grant accomplishment in a mere instant to those who desire the welfare of all beings; therefore, one should serve a woman.
Women are heaven; women are dharma; women alone are the supreme austerity.
Women are the Buddha; women are the Saṅgha; women are the Perfection of Wisdom.
They are conceptualized through the distinction of five colors according to their different names;
the woman who is blue in color is proclaimed as Dveṣavajrī.
A woman who is white and fair is considered to be Mohavajrī;
a woman who is yellow in color is the goddess Piśunavajrikā.
The woman who is red and white is proclaimed as Rāgavajrī;
the woman who is dark-complexioned is called Īrṣyāvajrī.
The one and only Blessed Lady Prajñā is established in five forms:
through flowers, incense, and so forth; through garments; and through the beauty of verse, prose, and their constituent parts.
Through conversation and prostrations, by holding the hands joined in the *sampuṭa-añjali* gesture,
and even through sight, touch, remembrance, and the performance of their words;
One should constantly worship Vajrayoginī with kisses and embraces;
when able, this should be performed with the body, and when unable, with speech and mind.
Thus honored by him, I am pleased and bestow all accomplishments;
having abandoned the form of the bodies of all women, I do not become anyone else.
"Abandoning the worship of women, there shall be no other worship for me;
by this propitiation, I am pleased for the sake of the practitioner's success."
Having meditated upon his own wife as being in every respect identical with my own entire form, he should desire her, always and everywhere, remaining constantly within the range of his vision.
Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, I am the bestower of enlightenment upon him;
therefore, he should be intent on propitiating me in every possible way.
Even if one should commit theft, or take the life of a living being,
or speak false words, or break an image and the like;
Whether he consumes what belongs to the Saṅgha, or what belongs to a stūpa, or the property of another,
the yogin who is intent upon my propitiation is not defiled by sins.
One should crush a louse with one's nail and even kill it if it is on a garment;
by this very practice, the practitioner should propitiate me.
One should not feel fear regarding sin or the miserable states such as the hells;
rather, one should inspire fear in the world for as long as power has not been attained.
Indeed, there is no evil whatsoever, nor is there any merit whatsoever;
the establishment of evil and merit exists only for the sake of protecting the minds of worldly beings.
Since everything is mind-only and its duration lasts but a single moment,
who indeed goes to hell, and who indeed proceeds to heaven?
Just as one dies from the fear of death caused by the poison of one's own imagination even in the absence of actual poison,
so too does one go to heaven or to a downward state.
Through such thorough comprehension, the wise attain even nirvāṇa;
indeed, nirvāṇa is of the nature of emptiness, like a lamp extinguished by the wind.
And upon its destruction, he too shall burn; he does not attain the state of enlightenment.
Therefore, having renounced everything, the practitioner should worship me alone.
I grant the fierce accomplishment (caṇḍasiddhi) in a mere instant; of this there is no doubt.
Then the Blessed One said to the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā:
"What would be the form of a fierce one, and what would his accomplishment be like?"
The Blessed One said: "The Yoginīs who have been proclaimed according to the distinction of five colors—
their respective husbands likewise [correspond] by the distinction of five colors."
All these who have been described by me as yoginīs are indeed fierce;
however, he who is the husband of blue complexion is known as Nīlācala.
For that husband who is white and fair is known by the name Śvetācala;
and that husband who is yellow in color is celebrated as Pītakācala.
Indeed, he who is red and white in complexion is declared to be Raktācala;
and he who is dark in complexion is known as Śyāmakācala.
He who is truly one becomes Caṇḍa, abiding in five forms;
this is declared to be Caṇḍa, and his accomplishment arises from steadfastness.
Extending as far as the limits of space, she abides in a divine form;
just as the accomplishment of Caṇḍa has been described, so too is Caṇḍī accomplished.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Essential Nature, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
Chapter A9.
Then the Blessed Lady said: "Blessed One, how should the ego-sense of wisdom and skillful means be cultivated?
The Blessed One replied:
The yogi, having placed a woman before him and intent on gazing at one another,
should maintain an upright body and meditate with a one-pointed mind.
Because they have the nature of the four bodies, there is not even the slightest difference;
however, apart from realization, a distinction between wisdom and means is maintained.
Death itself is said to be Dharma; the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga) is the intermediate state (antarābhava);
the emanation body (nirmāṇa) is form within the six realms of existence; and the enjoyment of desire is great bliss.
This one who possesses the nature of the four bodies exists in male form within the three realms;
and she who possesses the nature of the four bodies exists in female form within the three realms.
The Buddha, by virtue of having the nature of the four bodies, is indeed male;
and Prajñāpāramitā, established in all directions, is female.
He, however, should thus form the ego-sense: "I am indeed accomplished, abiding in my own form as the very nature of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa."
The knower of reality, having assumed the form of Caṇḍī as Siddhātmakāminī, should thus meditate with devotion for a long period of time.
Having abandoned all ritual actions, intent solely upon the service of the Vāmā,
one should remain with a mind focused exclusively on bliss until accomplishment is attained.
When the yogi has attained accomplishment, he becomes transparent and unimpeded;
manifested through the wind and mind, he is not seen at all by worldly people.
He is omniscient, all-pervading, omnipresent, and free from all afflictions;
for him there is neither disease nor old age, and death does not exist for him.
Neither poison nor water nor fire affects him;
nor do weapons or hosts of enemies ever prevail against him.
By the mere wish of the mind, the arising of all desires occurs;
at that very moment, it becomes effortless and is equal to a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
In all the world-systems, wherever he may be situated,
celestial palaces arise for him there, endowed with everything he desires.
He will have celestial women, beautiful and adorned with form and youth, as numerous as the stars in heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Śakra, Anaṅga, and all other gods,
as well as all living beings situated within the six realms of existence, become his servants.
Just as there is accomplishment for the yogin, so indeed is it for the yoginī;
men take the form of Vajradhara, and women are Vajrayoṣitas.
Then the Blessed Lady said: "Blessed One, how is it that great bliss arises in the body through the union of wisdom and means?
The Blessed One replied:
"The *lalanā* channel, which is established on the left, has the nature of wisdom."
And the *rasanā*, in the form of the means (*upāya*), is situated on the right.
The Avadhūtī is situated between the Lalanā and the Rasanā;
when the vital wind within the Avadhūtī is made into a single flavor with the semen.
From the junction of the head, it should fall through the vajra-opening into the interior of the woman's bhaga; and through the union of wisdom and means, the Caṇḍālī resides at the navel.
Like a lamp, it blazes; by that, the supreme semen is melted.
From that, a slight pleasure arises through slight application.
That is great because of its great yoga, and it is so by virtue of the intrinsic nature of reality;
that bliss is bound by which one becomes eternally [liberated] through the practice of yoga.
He shall indeed become the glorious Caṇḍaroṣa in this very life.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on Meditation, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekallavīra.
Chapter A10.
Then the Blessed One said: "Blessed One, can the state of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa be accomplished even apart from a woman, or is it not possible?
The Blessed One replied: "It is not possible, O Goddess."
The Blessed Lady said: "Blessed One, is it because happiness does not arise that [enlightenment] cannot be attained?
The Blessed One replied:
"Supreme enlightenment is not obtained merely by the arising of happiness."
That [state] is attained only through the arising of a specific excellence of happiness, and not otherwise.
And that effect does not arise without a cause;
and the cause is union with a woman, and never anything else.
Of all illusions, the illusion of a woman alone is praised;
he who overcomes that very illusion does not attain accomplishment.
Therefore, this separation from your wife must never be carried out,
even if such suffering, death, imprisonment, or fear should arise.
All of this is indeed endurable, but one must never abandon women;
for all women lead one to the attainment of Buddhahood through their joys.
Though shameless, fickle, and audacious, and always devoted to sensual desire,
these [goddesses] certainly grant accomplishment when served with one's whole being.
What more need be said of the nature of women? They even die out of love; what further can be said regarding their death through separation from their husbands alone?
Therefore, one should conceive of all women as goddesses in every respect—
even those conceived in the mind, or those made of wood, stone, and so forth.
For women, the male is the deity; for a man, the female is indeed the deity.
Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, there shall be mutual worship.
One should not worship any other deity, even one who is highly empowered;
therefore, the yogi, filled with compassion, should form a mandala before himself.
Having seated there a woman who is an embodiment of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā),
one should constantly worship her with flowers, as well as with lamps, incense, and so forth.
Thereafter, one should perform prostration through the yoga of the five mandalas;
then, one should perform circumambulation, whereby the worship of Caṇḍī is accomplished.
A woman should honor a man with respect and a mind of devotion;
the Victors have declared that such mutual worship should indeed be performed.
One should never revile a woman, nor should one avoid her when she seeks [one's favor];
one should speak sweet words and give what is appropriate.
One should pay homage with one's whole being so that the wicked one does not perceive it;
having heard this spoken by the Buddha, one should never abandon a woman under any circumstances.
He who would cause it to be otherwise is a sinner and experiences hell;
even death was already destined to occur, so what is gained by this separation from my wife?
The sādhana of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa is not accomplished by asceticism alone;
it becomes fruitless, and the stainless mind is afflicted by the web of delusion.
A person driven by desire may well not avoid sensual pleasures, yet he comes to live by wrong livelihood;
from living by wrong livelihood arises evil, and from evil comes rebirth in hell.
At the time of death, however, one who lives by wrong livelihood certainly attains [an evil rebirth]; there is no doubt.
For this very reason, the sons of the Conquerors accomplish spiritual perfection through desire alone.
Having likewise renounced the five objects of desire, one should not afflict oneself with asceticism;
one should perceive forms as they are encountered and hear sounds in the same way.
One should practice the smelling of fragrance, consume the most excellent flavor,
perform the touching of touch, and thus enjoy the five objects of desire.
One who is solely intent upon fierce wrath would become a Buddha even more swiftly;
there is no greater deception than this, nor any greater delusion than this.
You have not enjoyed human birth, youth, or all the pleasures of women;
rather, you see them as fruitless, having incurred a very great expense.
Devoted solely to sensual desire, they constantly serve their beloveds;
yet, upon seeing the state of fierce anger, they take refuge in the womb of a woman.
How could the wise son of Māyādevī abandon sleep, food, and even laughter for the sake of destroying the world's reproach?
Having again abandoned his inner apartments along with eighty-four thousand [attendants],
he went to the bank of the Nirañjanā river, manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood.
Having cast out the Māras, he did not depart in that manner from the perspective of ultimate reality;
for the Buddha remained established within the inner palace, accompanied by Gopā and dwelling in happiness.
Since true bliss is obtained from the union of the vajra and the lotus, enlightenment is attained through bliss; bliss does not arise from separation from women.
That separation which is brought about for the sake of removing the world's remorse is such that by it those worlds indeed attain the state of being disciplined by the Buddhas.
In that very same form, the Jina, the master of illusion, performs his dance;
yet, through all the Sūtras and Abhidharma, he utters censure against women.
One should speak of the various rules of training using language that conceals the reality;
one should also demonstrate nirvāṇa through the destruction of the five aggregates.
Then the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā asked: "Blessed One, who is the son of Queen Māyā, and who is Gopā?
The Blessed One replied:
"The son of Queen Māyā is myself, having attained the state of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa."
You alone are the Blessed Lady Gopā, whose very essence is the Perfection of Wisdom.
All women whatsoever are considered by me to be of your very form,
and all men indeed are proclaimed to be of my form.
This world, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means, exists in a twofold state.
Then the Blessed Lady said: "Blessed One, how is it that the śrāvakas and others revile women?
The Blessed One replied:
"All those known as śrāvakas and others who abide in the realm of desire [are so]."
They do not know the path to liberation; they always look upon women.
Where saffron and other such items are easily available, no value is placed upon them; whereas that which is situated at a distance possesses great worth.
Due to their connection with beginningless ignorance, these people lack faith and do not direct their minds toward reality; for this reason, even I have kept this concealed.
Nevertheless, in this Kali age, perhaps one among ten million—
a single being counted as such— will be devoted to faith and effort.
Everything has been spoken for his sake, for the swift accomplishment of awakening.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the Praise of Women, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
Chapter A11.
Then the Blessed One said: "Blessed One, are you possessed of passion or free from passion?
The Blessed One replied:
I am all, all-pervading, the creator of all, and the destroyer of all;
the Buddha who assumes every form, the agent, the withdrawer, the Lord, and the one who possesses bliss.
In whatever form beings are to be disciplined,
in that very form I abide for the sake of the world.
In one place he is a Buddha, in another a Siddha, and in another the Dharma or the Saṅgha;
in one place he is a preta, in another an animal, and in another one who has the form of a hell-being.
In some places I am a god and in others an asura; in some places I have the form of a human, and in some places I have the form of an immobile being—I am the universal form, without a doubt.
I am sometimes a woman, sometimes a man, and sometimes of neuter form; at times I am full of passion, at times full of hatred, at times deluded, and at times pure.
In some places I appear in an impure form, established in the form of mind;
my own mind is seen, and nothing else exists.
I am the distinction between reality and unreality; I am indeed both the produced and the producer.
I am the obstacle and I am the accomplishment, abiding in every form.
I am birth, I am death, I am disease, and I am old age;
I am merit, I am sin, and I am the fruit of those actions.
The entire world consists of the Buddha, and this very form is mine alone;
this should be understood by the yogi through the contemplation of reality in the form of the single flavor.
Then the Blessed Lady said: "Blessed One, is this form yours alone?
The Blessed One replied: "Your form is also of such a kind as all has been explained."
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded by you.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Chapter on the Universe, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekallavīra.
Chapter A12.
Then the Blessed One said: "Tell me the accomplishment of mantras, as well as those for pacification and enrichment."
And the practice of subjugation and attraction, as well as killing, expulsion, and so forth.
It brings about the destruction of poison, the destruction of disease, the immobilization of fire, swords, and the like,
as well as victory in battle and supreme scholarship.
O Lord, tell me with certainty: how is the accomplishment of yakṣiṇīs, the accomplishment of servants, messengers, spirits, and so forth, as well as power and manifold knowledge, achieved?
Then the Blessed One said:
"Abiding in the Caṇḍaroṣaṇa samādhi, one should begin the mantra practice.
First, one should accomplish the heart-mantra consisting of fifteen syllables."
This is known as the root mantra, which accomplishes all mantras;
wherever it remains written, there shall be well-being.
Whoever should uphold or recite it, their evil is uprooted;
by the mere remembrance of this mantra, the Māras flee in the ten directions.
Therefore, with every effort, one should accomplish this mantra.

Then, at that moment, all malevolent beings—pretas, vyāḍas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, mahoragas, and so forth—fled; all diseases were terrified; and all the grahas and other spirits were consumed by fire through the power of the mantra’s rays, while all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) became manifest.

Now follows its method of accomplishment: one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is completed. Then, beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight, one should recite it three times daily until the full moon. At the conclusion, having performed a great worship (*mahatī pūjā*), one should recite throughout the entire night, from the time of twilight until sunrise. Thereupon, this mantra becomes perfected (*siddha*). From that point forward, one performs all ritual actions (*sarvakarmāṇi*).

Now follows the practice for the Blessed One. One should have the Blessed One painted on a cloth. As before, in the center of a square maṇḍala, one should place the tenfold [deities] according to one's conviction. In front of that, beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times at each of the three junctions of the day. Then, at the end, on the full moon day, having performed worship according to one's means from the time of twilight until sunrise, fears will arise. One must not be afraid.
One should recite [the mantra] very quickly. Then the Blessed One comes in person. Having offered argha at his feet, one should prostrate and remain there.

Then the Blessed One said, "O [practitioner], what boon shall I grant you? The practitioner should say, "Grant me Buddhahood. Thereupon the Blessed One enters his body. As soon as he has entered, he becomes one who has the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, possesses the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), is a master of the thirteen stages (*trayodaśabhūmīśvara*), moves through divine palaces, is adorned by hosts of a hundred thousand celestial nymphs (*apsaras*), can assume any form at will, is omniscient, and resembles the Blessed One himself.

Alternatively, one may request whatever is desired—such as a sword, collyrium, pills, sandals, foot-unguents, sovereignty, sensual enjoyments, power, vidyā-mantras, wealth, poetic skill, scholarship, yakṣas, yakṣiṇīs, alchemy, the touch of mercury, or the transmutation of base metals—and the Blessed One grants it all.

Alternatively, having had a cloth painting (paṭa) of Ekallavīra painted, one should accomplish [the practice] as before. Here, on this cloth painting of Ekallavīra, Kṛṣṇācala should be depicted embraced by Dveṣavajrī; Śvetācala by Mohavajrī; Pītācala by Piśunavajrī; Raktācala by Rāgavajrī; and Śyāmācala by Īrṣyāvajrī. Alternatively, the Blessed One may be depicted alone, without a consort.

Alternatively, one should visualize the Bhagavatī alone from among the five. Then, having meditated upon oneself in the form of her husband, she should be accomplished as before. Or else, one should accomplish her by visualizing one's own wife in the form of the goddess. Once she is accomplished, she bestows even Buddhahood, let alone other accomplishments.

Alternatively, one should practice the sādhana of [the deity] standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, holding a sword and a noose. Or else, one should practice Sahaja Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa seated in the *sattvaparyaṅka* posture, embracing his own consort with both hands, which hold a sword and a noose. The accomplishment is as before. Thus is the accomplishment of the Blessed One from a painted cloth (*paṭa*). Alternatively, the accomplishment of an image made of wood and so forth should also be performed in this very same way.

Now, for the accomplishment of the sword (*khaḍgasādhana*), one should then, during the Puṣya asterism, take a sword made of high-quality steel or a blade made of strong wood according to one's preference. Having washed it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and anointed it with all types of perfumes, one should grasp it with both hands as before and recite the mantra for one month at the three junctions of the day. At the end of the month, having performed a great worship, one should recite throughout the entire night. At dawn, it blazes forth. One becomes a sword-vidyādhara, appearing like a youth of sixteen years, with hair curled into earrings;
one sports with the five objects of desire until the end of saṃsāra.

In this way, one should accomplish the vajra, the wheel, the trident, and so forth. In this way, one should accomplish a noose made of copper or other materials. In this way, one should accomplish a cloth painting, sandals, a sacred thread, garments, an umbrella, a manuscript of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, a manuscript of a tantra, and so forth. In this way, one should accomplish a drum, a mṛdaṅga drum, a lute, and so forth. In this way, one should accomplish a golden yakṣa, such as Jambhala, Māṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Cibi, Kuṇḍalin, and others; all of them will carry out one's command.

In this manner, one should accomplish a *gandharva* made of bamboo; a *garuḍa* made of anthill clay; the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Indra, Kāmadeva, and so forth—made of *devadāru* wood; a *rākṣasa* drawn with charnel-ground charcoal; a *preta* drawn with burnt *gaḍa*-fish lye; a human being made of *madana* wood; *Gaṇapati* made of ivory; *piśācas* such as Pīlupāla and others made of *śākhoṭaka* wood; and *ḍākinīs* such as Gaurīcaurī and others drawn with coral-fish lye.

One should accomplish the *vetāla* spirits such as Rāmadeva and Kāmadeva made from human bone; the *nāgas* such as Vāsuki and the *nāginīs* made from *nāgakeśara* wood; and the *yakṣiṇīs* such as Hārītī, Surasundarī, Naṭṭā, Ratipriyā, Śyāmā, Naṭī, Padminī, Anurāginī, Candrakāntā, Brahmaduhitā, Vadhū, Kāmeśvarī, Revatī, Ālokinī, Naravīrā, and others, made from *aśoka* wood.

One should accomplish the Śrīdevī made of *vaṭa* wood, the King made of *devadāru* wood, and the host of apsarases beginning with Tilottamā, Śaśidevī, Kāñcanamālā, Kuṇḍalahāriṇī, Ratnamālā, Ārambhā, Urvaśī, Śrībhūṣaṇī, Ratī, and Śacī. Likewise, one should accomplish the nine planets: Sūrya, Candra, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu. Similarly, one should accomplish the Bodhisattvas such as Lokeśvara, Vajrapāṇi, Mañjuśrī, and others.

In this way, one should accomplish the Buddhas, such as Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and others; likewise the spirits, such as Aparājita and others; likewise the messengers, such as Yamāri and others; likewise the servants, such as Vajrakaṅkāla and others; and likewise all beings, both women and men. All become obedient to one's command.

If it is not accomplished on the first occasion, then one should perform it a second time. If it is still not so, then one should begin the third occasion. If even then it is not so, due to some great evil committed previously, then one should press down with the left knee upon the right foot and recite until it is accomplished. Thereafter, it will succeed even for a slayer of a Brahmin.

In this regard, here is the interweaving of the mantra for the *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa-sādhana*: *oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa āgaccha āgaccha hūṃ phaṭ*. For the attainment of the sword and other [siddhis], one should append: "accomplish such-and-such for me. For the treading upon [the feet], however, one should append: "slay such-and-such, slay!"

By a single recitation, it burns away even all five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*). One should append: "Destroy all my sins. Likewise, in all instances of fear, it provides protection by mere recitation. One should append: "Protect, protect me! In this way, it brings about protection everywhere.

Then, having visualized a mustard seed, a mung bean, or a black gram as if it were glowing red-hot iron, one should consecrate it one hundred and eight times with one's own mantra and strike anyone seized by a *ḍākinī* or other spirits; they will all depart. At the time of striking, one should add the words, "Drive away the *ḍākinīs* and others!"

Then, having written the mantra inside an eight-petaled lotus on a pair of unbaked clay bowls with chalk and having enclosed it within them, one should wrap them with a fisherman’s net and hang them at the door. This provides protection for children; one should recite, "Protect, protect the child! while applying it.

Having fashioned a doll to be accomplished with *madanaka* (Euphorbia tirucalli) four fingers in length, one should write the mantra on birch bark (*bhūrja*) and insert it into its heart using mustard seeds and the like. Then, one should pin the mouth with a thorn. The mouth of the opponent becomes pinned. The formula "pin the mouth of Devadatta" should be applied accordingly.

One should bury it at a crossroads; in this way, one should nail down the feet. This paralyzes the coming and going [of the enemy]. One should apply the formula: "Nail down the feet of Devadatta. One should nail down the heart; this paralyzes the body. One should apply the formula: "Nail down the heart of Devadatta."

With a human bone-stake, or an iron one, or a constricting thorn, whichever limbs he stakes, those limbs of his become paralyzed and filled with intense pain; "Devadatta’s such-and-such limb shall be staked"—this is how it is to be applied.

If one buries it at the door of someone's house, that person is driven away. It should be applied as: "Drive Devadatta away. By casting consecrated cremation ashes upon the two door-panels, one causes [the person] to be driven away. It should be applied as: "Drive Devadatta away."
Having pinned a doll with thorns, one should recite [the mantra], applying the words "Kill Devadatta."

Having consecrated a sword or other such object one hundred and eight times with one's own mantra, one should engage in battle; one attains victory. Whatever purpose one has in mind when offering the sacrificial oblation (bali), that is accomplished for them.

For diseases such as malignant fevers and the like, one should empower a peacock feather one hundred and eight times with one's own mantra and wipe away the affliction. One should apply the formula: "Destroy the such-and-such disease of so-and-so. Thus, there will be the pacification of all diseases.
In the same way, one should wipe away the bite with both hands and palms, applying the mantra: "Destroy the poison of Devadatta. This renders it free of poison.

Having visualized him thus brought under control, dependent, returned to his own place, naked, with disheveled hair, and seeing him fallen at one's feet, one should recite the mantra. He becomes submissive. One should apply the formula: "And bring so-and-so under my control."
Thus, having visualized [the target] as drawn in as before, one should recite the mantra. [The target] becomes drawn in. The phrase "draw in so-and-so" is to be applied accordingly.
Having visualized oneself as completely filled with wealth, grain, and so forth, one should recite the mantra, adding: "Grant me nourishment."

Having written this mantra with a thorn upon a leaf enclosed between two triangles, one should consume it with betel leaf and five types of black pepper; it should be applied with the words, "Destroy all fevers."

During a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, one should fill a vessel with milk-rice or curd-rice, place it upon seven *aśvattha* leaves together with sugar and ghee, cover it with the seven leaves, and hold it firmly with both hands while reciting the mantra until [the planet] is released. One should then consume that food; one will attain a lifespan of five hundred years.

In this very same sequence, one may prepare yellow orpiment, *gorocanā*, or realgar, or else collyrium. When it is set ablaze, by means of a forehead mark (*tilaka*) or as an ointment (*añjana*), one becomes a *vidyādhara*. When it is reduced to smoke, invisibility (*antardhāna*) is attained. When it is heated until it emits warmth, subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) is achieved.

Alternatively, one should have an image of the serpent king Ananta made from *nāgeśvara* wood. Placing it face-down in the midst of water, one should recite the mantra while gazing at the sky. One should append the words: "Hara hara! O Ananta, cause rain to fall quickly! Then the deity will send down rain.

Then, having drawn Ananta out from the water and bathed him with milk, one should dismiss him. Then, while gazing at the cloud, one should recite the mantra; one should apply it [with the intent]: "Paralyze all winds and rain!"

Thus ends the ritual procedure for the eleven-and-a-half-syllable mantra. In this same manner, the ritual procedure for the second and third root mantras is established; this very same ritual procedure applies to the heart mantras as well.
