Having first written the root mantra on a *ketakī* leaf with a thorn, and having wrapped it with two threads of blue cloth, one should bind it upon the head, arm, neck, or back of the feverish person while placing the left foot [upon it], with a mind full of wrath, thinking: "I shall destroy the fever of such-and-such a person. This destroys all fevers.

At the time of binding, having turned the patient toward the east and having performed the ritual sprinkling (*nirmañcana*) with a bowl filled with burnt fish, cooked rice, liquor, and so forth, one should say: "Having consumed this, may all fevers and other ailments depart quickly; thus commands the Blessed Lord Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa! If you do not depart, then the Blessed One, being enraged, will cut you into pieces the size of sesame seeds with his sharp sword. Having said this, one should cast [the offering] in the southwest corner (*nairṛtakoṇa*). Thereupon, well-being ensues.

In this way, an offering (bali) should be given during afflictions such as all diseases and ḍākinīs. In all fears, it provides protection by the mere recitation [of the mantra]. Furthermore, it accomplishes everything stated in the root mantra. This same procedure applies to the second garland-mantra (mālāmantra) as well.

Having consecrated the offered ball of food with the third garland-mantra, one should give it; he becomes a granter of boons. Having consecrated a ball of cooked rice, one should give it at the time of twilight in a secluded place; whatever purpose one has in mind, all that is accomplished. The remaining ritual procedure is as before. One should perform it as before, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon, according to the previously stated rule.

The preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for *mālāmantras* consists of ten thousand recitations. For the specific mantras (*viśeṣamantra*) of the gods, the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is like that of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Just as it is for the Blessed One’s mantra-ritual, so it is for the goddesses. However, the distinction is that through the recitation of the *mālāmantra*, poetic skill and scholarship are swiftly attained.

The ritual procedure for the third root mantra is as follows: Having ascended to a bed and grasped the *liṅga* with the left hand, one should recite it one hundred and eight times while uttering the name of the woman she is intended for; she will come and fulfill one's desire. The mantra is: Oṃ vauheri [name] māyātu hūṃ phaṭ.

Having drawn a vulva on the ground with red ochre and pressing it down with the left hand, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times while mentioning the name of a woman; she will come.

Having consecrated a mustard seed seven times with the mantra, one should strike a person; that person becomes free from disease. One should perform the visualization mentally. Having recited the mantra over water, one should strike [the person]; blood flows forth. Having recited the mantra over a garment, one should wrap oneself in it; one becomes beloved by all people. Having recited the mantra over salt, if one gives it to someone for eating or drinking, one brings that person under one's control.

If one binds a rope made of cowhair around someone's neck after consecrating it with mantras, that person becomes a cow. Facing the sun, if one recites [the mantra] while mentioning someone's name, one draws that person toward oneself. If one binds a rope made of cat-hair around someone's neck, he becomes a cat. With a rope made of crow-tendons, one becomes a crow; with a rope made of human hair, one becomes a man; and with a rope made of woman's hair, one becomes a woman.

In this way, for whomever a rope is made from hair, body hair, and so forth, for that very person a transformation of form occurs. In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the lack of knowledge regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. The meaning is that immediately after death, the mind—which is like a bow—takes on the form of a body.

From that, consciousness arises. It is of six kinds: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Conjoined with these, ignorance sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, and conceptualizes.

Therefore, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). "Name" consists of the four [aggregates] beginning with sensation (*vedanā*); "form" is form itself. The consciousnesses are exactly as previously described. Form consists of the four primary elements: earth is heaviness and solidity; water is fluidity and moisture; fire is heat and maturation; wind is contraction, expansion, lightness, and motion.

By binding the root of *varāhakrāntā* to the ear during the period following menstruation, a woman becomes pregnant.

One should eat *kalambī* vegetable for the increase of semen; by eating sweet curd, there is an increase of semen; by consuming semen and blood, there is an increase of semen; and by mixing a woman's excrement with her urine and drinking it, there is an increase of semen.

One should consume *āmalakī* powder at the end of the day with water, ghee, or honey; it is beneficial for the eyes, promotes youthfulness, and generates wisdom. One should likewise eat *āmalakī* powder and sesame powder with ghee and honey; the result is the same.
One should eat the root of *gorakhataṇḍulā* together with *aśvagandhā*, sesame, and barley, having made them into a uniform mass with jaggery; this generates youthfulness.
One should consume the powder of *arjuna* bark with milk or other liquids; by practicing this for a year, one attains a lifespan of three hundred years.

One should drink one pala of āmalakī juice with one karṣa of bākucī powder in the morning; when it has been digested, one should eat a meal of milk. By this, one attains a lifespan of five hundred years within a month.
One should drink one karṣa of Bākucī powder with buttermilk, water, sour gruel, or milk; after six months, one will be endowed with youthfulness.
One should consume the powder of *muṇḍarī* with clarified butter; within three weeks, one attains the appearance of a sixteen-year-old.

One *pala* of the powder of *sanabīja* and one *pala* of red *śāli* rice should be cooked with two *śarāva* measures of milk from a cow of uniform color. First, having reduced one *śarāva* of the milk to its essence, one should add the *sana* and other ingredients and cook it. Then, one should consume it. Once digested, one should eat with milk. One must avoid wind and sun. For three weeks, the procedure is as follows, and the subsequent procedure is likewise. Thereafter, the hair and so forth fall out and grow back again. Thus, free from wrinkles and graying hair, one lives for five hundred years.
One should consume the root of *raktoccaṭa*, the size of a cat's footprint, with ghee and honey; likewise for the fruit.

One should prepare pills the size of an *uḍumbara* fruit from the powders of *āmalakī*, *harītakī*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *pippalī*, black pepper, and iron, mixed with honey and sugar. Then, one should consume a single pill. By doing so for one month, one attains a lifespan of three hundred years.
One should eat one *pala* of *kumārī* combined with ghee and curd; within seven days, one's lifespan becomes three hundred years.
One should eat barley, sesame, *aśvagandhā*, *nāgabalā*, and black gram with double the amount of jaggery; one becomes possessed of great strength.
One should consume *bhadrālīguṇḍaka*—three times the amount of *harītakī*—with water or other liquids; thus one will become possessed of great strength.
One should visualize oneself everywhere in the form of the deity, and one should empower the medicinal herb with the mantra.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on the increase of semen and so forth, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
Chapter A18:
Then the Blessed One said: Having ground the root of the castor plant with sour gruel, one should rub it on the head; this destroys headache.
One should fill the ear with lukewarm urine of a goat, a cow, or a human, mixed with rock salt; this destroys ear diseases. Alternatively, one may apply dried monkey oil.

One should prepare pills with *kataka*, *pippalī*, *āmalakī*, *haridrā*, and *vacā* using cold water. By applying this as a collyrium (*añjana*), all eye diseases are destroyed; or one may apply it as a collyrium with honey and *pippalī*.
One should anoint the earwax with honey; this destroys night-blindness.

Now, one should apply a collyrium made from these; it destroys all eye diseases. Having ground oil, rock salt (*saindhava*), and the root of *dūrvā* grass in *kāñjika* vinegar within a bronze vessel (*kāṃsa*), one should recite the mantra; this destroys eye pain.
Having smelled the fruit of *ghoṣa*, one should drink the root of *kaṅkola* with rice-water and apply it as a nasal drop (*nasya*). Blood will not flow from the nose.
By chewing the root of *śephālikā*, the uvula is destroyed.
The root of *guñjā* destroys dental caries.
One should cook cow’s ghee, cow’s milk, and *karkaṭapada*; by anointing the feet with this, dental caries are destroyed.
Having ground together radish seeds, priyaṅgu, red sandalwood, and kuṣṭha, one should apply it as an ointment; thereby the *markaṭī* and other such ailments are destroyed.
One should drink one *pala* of dried deer meat with goat’s milk; this destroys the disease of consumption (*kṣaya*).
The consumption of buffalo curd and rice destroys diarrhea, as does the eating of sour rice.
One should drink two parts of *kuṭaja* bark along with one part each of black pepper, jaggery, and ginger, mixed with cow's buttermilk; this destroys *grahaṇī*.

One should consume equal parts of *āmalakī*, *pippalī*, *citraka*, fresh ginger, old jaggery, clarified butter, and honey; this destroys chronic cough and dyspnea. Likewise, the powder of *harītakī* taken with honey has the same effect.
One should eat barley gruel with *khadirī* vegetables; there will be a destruction of abdominal diseases.
One should drink fresh ginger and cumin with curd or with whey, combined with salt; this is a destroyer of dysuria.
One should eat equal parts of sugar and barley-alkali, or drink a decoction of the root of *Śaubhāñjana*; the urinary stone (*aśmarī*) will fall away.
One should drink harītakī, citraka, and ginger with buttermilk; this is a destroyer of splenic enlargement.
One should eat cumin with jaggery; thus fever and wind are destroyed.
One should drink barley-alkali with curd; this destroys *āmavāta*.
Having added the three pungents, viḍaṅga, and rock salt, one should drink the lukewarm scum; the digestive fire is kindled and the worms are destroyed.
One should eat *harītakī* with jaggery; hemorrhoids will be destroyed. One should eat *harītakī* with ginger; there is a destruction of rheumatism caused by undigested matter (*āmavāta*).

By grinding dūrvā grass with turmeric and applying it as a paste, skin diseases (kaccha) are destroyed. By this very same method, one may also eliminate ringworm (dadrū), boils (visphoṭaka), wounds from dog bites, and other such ailments.
Having ground the root of *kāsamardaka* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should likewise drink molasses with pungent oil; thus, asthma is destroyed.
One should consume the bark of the Arjuna tree with ghee and other substances; this results in the destruction of heart pain.
Having burnt bilva fruit, one should eat it with jaggery; this destroys bloody diarrhea.
One should drink the juice of *mātuluṅga* with jaggery; the colic pain is destroyed.
One should administer a nasal drop (nasya) of jaggery and ginger; it destroys all phlegm disorders.
One should anoint with honey the *ketaka* flower; this destroys all eye diseases.
By rubbing together sour gruel, oil, rock salt, and the roots of dūrvā grass in a bronze vessel and applying it as an ointment, eye pain is destroyed.
One should eat jaggery with ghee; wind, bile, phlegm, skin diseases, and other ailments will be destroyed.
One should consume the powder of triphalā with ghee and honey; this destroys all diseases.
One should lick the powder of *harītakī* with ghee and honey at the transition between meals; this destroys wind and phlegm disorders.

Having dried and powdered the five parts of *vāsaka*, *vacā*, *brahmī*, and *pippalī*, one should prepare pills with rock salt (*saindhava*) and honey. Then, one should consume them at the evening mealtime. Wind-phlegm (*vāta-śleṣman*) is destroyed, and the voice becomes sweet.
One should prepare pills with *brahmī*, *vacā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *pippalī*, *harītakī*, *vāsaka*, and *khadira* mixed with honey and consume them; the result is likewise [efficacious].
One should consume equal parts of yavānī, śuṇṭhī, harītakī, and saindhava; this destroys all types of indigestion.
One should drink the juice of *guḍūcī* with honey; in one three-month period, there is the destruction of urinary disorders (*prameha*).
One should drink milk mixed with powdered long pepper (pippalī), ghee, and honey; fever, heart disease, cough, and other ailments will be destroyed.
One should grind the roots of *lajjālu* and *śarapuṅkha* with water and apply it as an ointment; one should also consume the root of *guḍūcī*. This destroys sinus ulcers (*nāḍīvraṇa*).
One should eat ginger with alkali of barley; hunger arises.
One should drink the seed of *jayantī* with black pepper for three days; this destroys sinful diseases.

Triphalā, nalikā, black earth, bhṛṅgarāja, the sour seed of the mango, iron powder, and fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika)—with these one should produce *pāmana* (a skin condition). Then, having fumigated the hair with guggulu, one should rub it with that [mixture]. Having bound it for seven days, one should leave it there. This is hair-dyeing.
Having cooked cow’s ghee with peacock bile and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, one should administer it as a nasal drop (*nasya*); this effects the blackening of the hair within seven days.

One should prepare a decoction of *punarnavā* and *raṇḍā* with sixteen parts of water and retain one part. Then, having strained it, one should add the powder of white *guṇḍā*. Next, one should apply one *śarāva* measure of oil. By massaging the hair with this, the hair is dyed.

Having powdered equal parts of bhūmividārī, trikaṭu, and sulphur, and having placed them inside a wick, one should take mustard oil by means of a downward-pointing burning wick and apply it continuously as nasal drops twice; thereby, wrinkles and graying hair are destroyed.
By applying a plaster of kuṣṭha with this squeezed juice, there is relief.

By means of a *ghaṭayantra* (pot-press) containing one *tolaka* of mercury mixed with one *māṣaka* of fragrant black gram (*kāṣamāṣaka*) recently kneaded with butter, along with a lump of *śāliñcī* and *loṇikā*, and sealed inside with a lid (*mūṣikā*) over a bed of sand, the binding of the mercury occurs through the application of fire. By its consumption, the destruction of consumption (*kṣaya*) and other diseases is achieved.

Having taken the first excrement of a calf, one should have it made into pills. One should grind *piṇḍatagara* root and wrap [the pill] with it. Having consumed one pill, one may consume poison; it will not take effect.

Having ground together the seeds of the jambu tree, the seeds of the citron, and the seeds of the śirīṣa tree, one should cook milk-rice with goat's milk; one should eat it with ghee. For as long as one fortnight, hunger will not occur.
By applying a paste of āmalakī, kuṣṭha, utpala, māṃsī, and balā, thin hair becomes thick.
Having burnt dog's teeth with internal smoke and mixed them with milk and ghee, one should apply it; even poorly grown hairs will grow back.
Having placed the male organ in coconut water for a few moments, one should apply *surasunna-guṇḍaka*; the disease of men is destroyed.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on the removal of diseases and old age, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekallavīra.
Chapter A19: Then the Blessed One said:
"Having made a pill from the root of the white Aparājitā with semen, a woman is brought under control by means of a forehead mark."
Having extracted the penis with *brahmadaṇḍī*, *vacā*, and honey, one may desire a woman; she comes under one's control.
One should give the root of *daṇḍotpala*, *kuṣṭha*, and betel; likewise, one should give *brahmadaṇḍī*, *viḍaṅga*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *nāgakeśara* with betel. [The person] becomes submissive.
Having ground donkey semen and lotus filaments together, one should smear the penis and engage in sexual union; [the woman] becomes submissive.

Taking *gorocanā* from a cow that has not been bitten by insects and mixing it with the juice of the *svayambhū* flower to form a *tilaka*, one achieves subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Likewise, by applying collyrium made from the root of *bhṛṅgarāja* mixed with one's own semen, the same result is attained.
One should smear a creeper of white karavīra with the blood of a wolf or a jackal; having fumigated it with smoke from a cremation ground, one may kill a woman, or she shall become submissive.

She upon whose head the crest of a peacock, the tongue of a crow, the remains of offerings, and powdered cloth from a corpse are placed becomes submissive. Likewise, by anointing the penis with the root of *viṣṇukrāntā* during sexual union, she is brought under control.

One should collect the fruit of the *dhustūra* under the Puṣya asterism; its bark under Āśleṣā; its leaf under Hasta; its flower under Citrā; and its root under Mūla. One should prepare pills from these equal parts of powder mixed with honey. Having bound them in a cloth, one should dry them. They should be administered with betel leaf. This brings about subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) when used with conch-shell powder.
If one writes the name of a woman with the juice of *mekākṣī* using the index finger of a mad dog, saying, "Let so-and-so come," she arrives.
One should heat a peacock’s crest in a smokeless fire and apply it with the five impurities at the beginning of digging and other such tasks; [the target] becomes submissive.

Having cultivated the root of Aparājitā under the Puṣya asterism and having smeared a cloth with human oil, one should cause soot to fall into a human skull; by means of this oil-and-collyrium, one brings both women and men under control.
One should administer the root of *daṇḍotpala* together with the five impurities; this brings [the person] under one's control.
One should administer viḍaṅga, tagara, and kuṣṭha with wine; it destroys indigestion.
One should apply collyrium made from the powder of realgar, nāgakeśara, priyaṅgu, and gorocanā to the eyes; this is a means of subjugation.
One who has applied a tilaka made from musk, lajjā, dhūstūra, and sahadevā brings the three worlds under his control.

Oṃ calacitte cili cili culu culu reto muñca muñca svāhā. Having placed a red karavīra flower upon one’s own liṅga, one should recite this mantra one thousand times. By piercing a copper vessel with the name [of the woman] interwoven [with the mantra] and reciting the mantra before her while it is being whirled, she becomes submissive.

Having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) ten thousand times without the name, [the mantra is]: *namaś caṇḍālī amukīṃ vaśīkuru svāhā*. This constitutes the service (*sevā*) of ten thousand repetitions. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should empower cremation ashes one hundred and eight times and apply them to the head of a woman; she will become submissive.
Taking the penis of a goat or the tail of a crow, one should tie it with cemetery threads around the waist; this is a method for the suppression of semen.
With the mind focused solely on true bliss, one should engage in sexual union through the application of fortitude;
remaining always as if motionless, this is the supreme method for the retention of semen.
One should bind the root of the plant called *sitakokilā* or that of *dhustūra*,
or the root of *śvetaśarapuṅkha*, for the purpose of arresting semen.
If one should consume hemp root, *śatī* root,
or *surasunnaka* before sexual intercourse, it is the supreme method for the immobilization of semen.
Having carved out a karañja fruit, one should fill it with mercury;
by binding it around the waist with threads, it is the supreme means for retaining semen.
One should light a lamp with boar oil and a wick made from the root of a white *arka* plant dyed with lac. This is for the immobilization of semen (*śukrastambhana*).
Alternatively, one may cook safflower oil and smear the soles of the feet with it; this is a method for the suppression of semen.
By applying a plaster made from the root of *kākajaṅghā*, white lotus, and the honey of lotus filaments, there is the immobilization of semen.
Having wrapped the root of *viṣṇukrāntā* with a lotus leaf, one should bind it around the waist. This is a method for the suppression of semen (*śukrastambhana*).
Having ground yellow orpiment, rasāñjana, mercury, long pepper, rock salt, kuṣṭha, and the excrement of a pigeon, applying it as a suppository in the anus results in the immobilization of semen.
Having taken the horn of an upward-facing bull and rubbing it, one should smear the penis; the penis becomes erect.

Having ground the root of *kapikacchu* with goat’s urine, one should smear it on the penis, massage it, and then pull [the penis] three times; paralysis occurs. Cessation occurs by washing with hot water.
Having filled a cowrie shell with mercury, one should place it in the mouth; this is for the immobilization of semen.
One should saturate *indravāruṇī* with goat's urine for seven days; by rubbing [the penis] with that, it becomes rigid.

Having ground the root of *oṣaṇī*, the root of *kāmācī*, and the seed of *dhustūra* with camphor-water and having smeared it upon the penis, one may desire a woman; she will become moistened. Likewise, by grinding rock salt (*saindhava*), borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), camphor, and *ghoṣaka* into a powder and smearing it on the penis with honey, the same result occurs.
Having ground pigeon dung with honey and smeared it on the penis, one may desire her; she will emit [fluid].
At the moment of sexual union, one should cause a woman to eat the root of the *kāmācī* plant with betel; she will then discharge [her fluids].

Having mixed the juice of ripe tamarind with rock salt and smeared it on one’s own index finger, one should insert it into her bhaga and move the channel of Vajradhātvīśvarī until she emits [the fluid].
By applying a plaster of camphor, borax, mercury, *hastipippalī*, and honey, a woman discharges [fluid].
Having chewed the root and leaves of the *rāmadūtī* plant and inserted it into the penis, one should engage in sexual union; [the semen] flows.

Having ground radish on the Jayantī day and mixed it with rice-water, by applying it as an ointment to the womb during sexual intercourse, a barren woman will bear children; of this there is no doubt.
Having ground the seeds of the *palāśa* tree, one should apply them with honey and clarified butter; by drinking this, a barren woman will undoubtedly give birth to a child with red moles.
One should apply the powder of locusts and grasshoppers to a loose vulva; it becomes firm.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, concerning the immobilization of semen and other [rites], in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
Chapter A20. Then the Blessed Lady said this to the Blessed One:
"The skill in mantras, yantras, and so forth, has been explained through various classifications."
Furthermore, O Lord, I desire to hear more; such is my curiosity.
Grant me now the complete yoga of the vital breaths, as well as the characteristics of time,
the true nature of the bodily machine, and its purification.
Then the Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Goddess, that you have made this request here. Therefore, I shall now fully proclaim the collection of all vidyās."

Oṃ, O you whose face is formidable with flames! Ha ha! O Halāhalavajrā, Suvajrā! Flash forth, flash forth! Cause [all] to flash forth, cause [all] to flash forth! Paralyze, paralyze all clouds, winds, and rain! Shatter, shatter! Yaḥ yaḥ yaḥ! Dry up, dry up all water! Hūṃ phaṭ! While reciting this mantra, one should gaze at the sky with a piercing look. It destroys wind, clouds, and the like.
Oṃ phetkāra pheṃ pheṃ ha ha hā hā pheṭ | This is the mantra for sporting in the cremation ground.

Oṃ, to the Lord of All Knowledge, the destroyer of all other diagrams and mantras; terrify, terrify all ḍākinīs! Bind, bind! Nail down, nail down with bliss! Hūṃ phaṭ! This is the mantra for entering cities and sacred precincts.
Oṃ hili hili phuḥ phuḥ! Having consecrated the earth with this mantra, one should apply the dust; the serpent flees.
"Mother! Mother!"—by saying this, the tiger flees.
"Vedu ā! Vedu ā!"—with these words, the elephant flees.
"Terli ā terli ā"—by this, the goiter flees away.
Oṃ hrīṃ baṭukanātha caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ! By threatening with the left index finger while reciting this, dogs flee.
Oṃ Yamāntaka hrīḥ strīḥ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ trāsaya trāsaya caṇḍa pracaṇḍa hūṃ phaṭ! By this [mantra], the buffalo flees.
Oṃ yamamardane mardaya mardaya caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ! By this [mantra], sinful diseases flee away.
Oṃ krośaṇe saṃkrośaṇe bhedanāya hūṃ phaṭ! Having thus consecrated it with this mantra, one should give water; the pain of the stake (śūla) flees away.
Oṃ trāsane mohanāya hūṃ phaṭ! By this [mantra], protection is obtained through the binding of the topknot.

Oṃ acale saṃcale, nail the mouth of [Name]! Hūṃ phaṭ! Having fashioned a four-finger-sized effigy out of *madana* wood, having written [the mantra] upon birch bark with yellow orpiment, and having inserted it into the mouth of that effigy, one should nail it shut. One should bury it at a crossroads; this nails the mouth of the opponent.
Oṃ, O shatterer of all Māras, nail down the feet of [Name]! Hūṃ Phaṭ! Having inserted it into the heart as before, one should nail down the feet; this paralyzes their coming and going.

Oṃ, O you of deformed face, destroyer of the enemy’s forces! Break, break! Paralyze, paralyze! With the vajra-noose, bind, bind so-and-so together with his army! Hūṃ phaṭ khaḥ gaḥ ha hā hi hī pheṃ pheṃ! Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ! Having cast [the effigy] as before, one should drive stakes into the eight limbs of the commander of the enemy army. Placing it face-downward in the center of a hearth, one should bury it. This paralyzes the arrival of the enemy army.

Oṃ daha daha paca paca matha matha jvara jvara jvālaya jvālaya śoṣaya śoṣaya gṛhṇa gṛhṇa jvala jvala | Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Having written the name of the one called Devadatta, measuring eight finger-breadths, upon a cloth from a cemetery using poison and black mustard seeds, having wrapped it with the garland-mantra (mālāmantra), and having placed it within the heart of a doll made of *madana* wood, one should insert it into the midst of *snuhī* wood. Then: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, cause such-and-such a person to be seized by fever! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Reciting this, one should heat [the effigy] in a cremation fire, or in a fire of *khadira* or *badara* wood; thus one causes the enemy to burn.

Oṃ jaya jaya parājaya nirjitayantre hī hī hā hā sphoṭaya sphoṭaya ucchādaya ucchādaya śīghraṃ karma kuru kuru | Oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ | Having written this on a cloth from a cremation ground and wrapped it with blue thread, one should wear it on the arm, the neck, the head, or the waist. No other mantra will prevail [against it].

Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, swallow, swallow! Kha kha! Eat, eat! Dry up, dry up! Kill, kill! Slay, slay so-and-so! Hūṃ phaṭ! Having written this on a cloth from a cemetery, one should place it as before inside a doll, nail it with a bone stake or an iron stake the size of a finger, and bury it face down in a cemetery. Within seven days, he causes death.

Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, expel so-and-so! Hūṃ Phaṭ! Taking the droppings of a crow from a neem tree, one should burn them in a funeral pyre. One should then cast that ash, consecrated eight hundred times with the mantra, upon the roof of the house. One should visualize [the enemy] mounted on a camel, bound by a noose, and being led toward the southern direction. Thus, one causes expulsion.

Oṃ! O Hater, O Vajra of Hatred, cause [Name] to be hated by [Name]! Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ! Taking the dust from two fighting dogs, one should strike two effigies of the targets; they will cause mutual hatred.

Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hrīṃ hrīṃ hroṃ! O you of terrible form! Caṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa! Strike, strike! Slay, slay! Smash, smash! Ha ha ha ha! Flash forth, flash forth! Cause to flash forth, cause to flash forth! Pin, pin! Render unconscious, render unconscious! Paralyze, paralyze! [Strike] so-and-so! Hūṃ phaṭ! Having drawn a tortoise on birch bark with lacquer to a size of six finger-breadths, one should place the syllable *hrīḥ* on its four legs and the syllable *plī* in the middle of its mouth.

Then, having drawn a figure of excrement in a pit and the practitioner behind it, one should encircle them with the *mālāmantra* and commence worship and praise. Having placed [the vessel] upon a brick, one should cover it with the *kūrma-catuṣka* (the fourfold tortoise). Encircling it with a red thread, one should cast it toward the feet. One should strike with the left foot, saying "Bring so-and-so under my control," seven times. This easily paralyzes the enemy.
Oṃ cili mili lalite hūṃ phaṭ. The contraction of the eyes is destroyed.

Oṃ cchrīṃ cchrīṃ cchrīṃ! Dry it up, dry it up! Bind the flow, bind it! Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ! One should bury a peg made of cow-bone, measuring seven finger-breadths in length and consecrated one hundred and eight times, in a cow-pen; then milk will not flow.

Oṃ, O wielder of the vajra, let the vajra fall! The Lord of the Gods commands: blaze, blaze! Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ! A vajra made of clay from an anthill, consecrated one hundred and eight times, should be hidden in a shop; the merchandise will perish.

Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ traṃ yūṃ, O crusher of Yama, draw [him] forth, draw [him] forth! Agitate, agitate! O fulfiller of all desires, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! One should draw the deity upon a birch-bark leaf—two-armed, resembling saffron in color, holding a noose and a goad in his hands, fierce with intense passion. One should inscribe the syllables of the mantra with elephant ichor, lac, menstrual blood, and saffron: *oṃ* on the head, *hrīṃ* at the heart, *klīṃ* at the navel, and *traṃ* at the genitals.

Then, having encircled it with the *mālāmantra* and wrapped it with a red thread, one should place it inside a hollowed-out skull-cup made from the joined halves of a woman’s and a man’s cranium; having filled it with ghee and honey and bound it with *madana* resin, one should bury it at the head of [the target] while tying it with a red thread. Treading upon it with the left foot, one should recite the mantra. With twenty-five thousand recitations, the city will be thrown into turmoil.

Oṃ ākarṣa ākarṣa, mohaya mohaya, bring such-and-such a woman under my control, svāhā! Having made a fine powder of a worm from the stomach and formed it into a pill with the blood from the ring finger of one who has had sexual intercourse, one should empower it with this mantra and give it to be consumed in food or drink; she will be brought under control.
The two wings of a bee with fluttering feathers,
the two tusks of a corpse, and a garland—
when one's limbs are dusted with this powder, [the desired effect follows].
At every step she runs, her limbs fainting.
Oṃ śvetagṛdhṛṇi khāhi viṣaṃ ca ruṣaṃ ca khaḥ khaḥ ha ha saḥ saḥ | Oṃ Caṇḍamahāsenājñāpayati svāhā | Alternatively: Oṃ saṃkāriṇi dhraṃ hāṃ hūṃ haṃ haḥ | This destroys all poison.
Oṃ nāgāri vāmanaharaḥ phaṭ! By means of earth consecrated with this mantra, or by means of a written inscription at the door, snakes will not enter.
Oṃ āṇe kāṇe, bring such-and-such a person under control, svāhā! Subjugation is achieved by offering fragrant white flowers.
Homage to the one free from passion, Maitreya with the lion’s gaze, svāhā! By washing the eyes with water consecrated by this [mantra], cataracts are destroyed.
Oṃ saphara khaḥ! Eat the powder; it shall not take effect.

By the speed of the Sun’s chariot, by the power of Vāsudeva, and by the flapping of Garuḍa’s wings, let the poison go to the earth, svāhā! This destroys the poison of serpents, scorpions, crabs, and the like.

Oṃ cāmuṇḍe ajite aparājite rakṣa rakṣa svāhā! Having consecrated a neṣṭuka-grass bundle seven times with this mantra, one should throw it in the four directions and place one at one's own location. Oṃ jambhanī stambhanī mohanī sarvaduṣṭapraśamanī svāhā! Thieves will not appear.

Homage to Caṇḍamahākrodha! Hulu hulu! Culu culu! Stay, stay! Bind, bind! Delude, delude! Strike, strike! Mṛte hūṃ phaṭ! By reciting this over flowers and other offerings and giving them away, one brings others under control.
Homage to the Three Jewels! Oṃ ṭaḥ suvismare svāhā! By means of a strip of *ketakī* leaf, one destroys all fevers.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, concerning the various methods of piercing and the application of yantras and mantras, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.

Chapter A21. Then the Blessed One said: "Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, O you who reveal all illusions, display all illusions! Be free from obstacles! Hūṃ Phaṭ! Having meditated upon Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa with this [mantra], one should perform everything.

Having smeared a cloth with the sap of the *uḍumbara* tree until it is without gaps, one should grind resin (*sarjarasa*) with oil, mix it into that [sap], and fashion a wick. When ignited with water, the lamp burns steadily.
At night, having rubbed two pieces of *varaṭa* wood together, one displays flashes of lightning by means of the syllable *hūṃ*.
By lighting a wick dyed with lac and mixed with the powder of dead leeches, women become naked upon seeing it.
By anointing the ears and eyes with ghee, one achieves self-protection.

One should cut off the tail of a *halāhala* serpent. While it writhes naked with its hair disheveled, one should make it dance. By lighting a lamp with wicks made from cloth dyed with lac and mixed with four *māṣaka* measures of that [serpent] powder and one *māṣaka* each of the five parts of the *dhustūra* plant, everyone dances upon seeing it. Self-protection is as before.
If one places the root of the śākhoṭaka tree and the root of the baheḍī tree together in the house, a quarrel will occur.

If a *guṇḍaka* seed placed in the middle of a *dhūstūra* flower is thrown into the midst of fragrant flowers and merely smelled, a headache occurs; liberation [from it] comes by means of a nasal application (*nasya*) of fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).

A bed made from the womb of a *kukkurī* (female dog) fumigated with that [substance] and wrapped in a peacock feather, when whirled around with the right hand, removes [the poison]; with the left hand, there is liberation.

Having written the mantra on a mango leaf with the blood from a crow’s heart using its wing as a pen, one should cast it into the excrement of a person; that person will be eaten by crows. Oṃ kākakuhanī kruddhanī devadattaṃ kākena bhakṣāpaya svāhā!
Having made a pit in the shape of a vulva and having placed therein the excrement of a woman mixed with the urine of a scorpion, one should conceal it; its path will become painful.
By anointing with sesame oil treated with the milk of *snuhī*, the hairs become white; when they have fallen out, there is liberation.
The *virālī* (spider) womb-bed and the woman’s womb-bed—by means of incense from both, no painting is seen on the wall; by means of honey-incense, there is liberation.

If the camel’s cheek is free of foam and urine, one should saturate yellow orpiment many times with it, smear it on the hand, and draw; the painting will not be seen. By washing the hand, there is release.
From the incense of *strīgarbhaśayyā*, one weeps strangely; by means of *guggulu* incense, there is liberation.
By anointing the eyes with the oil of a frog, serpents are seen within the beams of one's house.
By offering powdered fragrant substances into the fire of an extinguished lamp, it flares up again.
Having rubbed the feet with the fat of the *muṇḍirī*, *sevāla*, leeches, and frogs, and having wrapped them in a plantain leaf, one does not burn when walking upon glowing coals.
One should eat the root of *snuhī* with jaggery; sleep will ensue.
One should bind the root of the *kāmācī* plant to the topknot; sleep ensues.
By grinding the root of *nāgadamanī*, the root of *droṇapuṣpaka*, and *haridrātaṇḍula* together, and applying them as an ointment, one gains victory in the examination of water.
By digging for a globule of asafoetida at the root of a silk-cotton tree, one causes the falling of flowers.
One should administer *kāṅguṣṭha* with wine or betel; it becomes a purgative.
One should eat the milk of *snuhī*, the seeds of *arka*, and the powder of woodworms with molasses; blood will flow.
One should smear the nose of a horse with the powder of a muskrat; it will not take food. By washing it with sandalwood and applying nasal drops, there is release from this state.

One should bind the root of the *ketakī* to the head, the root of the date palm (*kharjūra*) to the hand, and the root of the palmyra palm (*tāla*) to the mouth. Under the constellation Puṣya, one should uproot [the plant] while standing in the northern direction. Having become naked with hair disheveled, one should grind a small portion of these three together and drink it; then no blow from a weapon will occur.
One should prepare a pair of sandals filled with Śyonāka seeds and covered with deerskin; [the wearer] does not sink in water.
Having chewed *oṣaṇī* and placed it on the surface of the tongue, one is not burned by the application of a heated plowshare.
From drinking *hastiśuṇḍī* mixed with *sūtakakṣāra*, there is a miscarriage of the fetus.

Having uprooted the root of the white *śarapuṅkha* during the *puṣya* asterism and having processed it with cow's ghee, one should bind it to the head and other parts; this wards off the falling of arrows and the fear of thieves.
Having mounted leather sandals with the fat of a vulture and the fat of an owl, one travels very great distances both going and returning.

On an auspicious day at twilight, one should consecrate a mustard seed that has not been struck by a weapon; then, having become naked and with hair disheveled, one should take it with the left hand and not place it on the ground. Furthermore, protection should be performed for the Blessed One with the Mālā-mantra.

With the blood of whichever [being] one should repeatedly perform the sprinkling, with its flesh the raising [of the image], with the essence of its bone the oil, and with its ashes the nourishment; having planted it in its skull, one should diligently perform the sprinkling with its fat, blood, flesh, and so forth, as well as fumigation and eye-ointment, and again and again provide protection and offerings.
Having placed a ripened fruit in the mouth, one should contemplate it as being of that same nature; one becomes just like that.

By wrapping [the object] with the three metals, one attains invisibility. In this regard, these are the three metals: three *māṣas* and three and a half *guñjās* for each; specifically, three *māṣas* according to the sun, moon, and fire [proportions]. Copper: 3 *māṣas*, 2 *tī* (or *tolas*); Silver: 4 (? *māṣas*, 2 *tī*; Gold: 3 *māṣas*, 5 (? *tī*.

Having drawn the image of the target upon a human skull using *gorocanā* mixed with red pigment, and having inscribed their name therein interspersed with the mantra, one should smear it with scented water, enclose it between a second skull, wrap it with a thread from a corpse, tie it with beeswax, and recite the mantra. One should heat it over charcoal from a funeral pyre at night until the beeswax melts. This brings even a celestial maiden (*surakanyā*) under one's power. OṂ ĀKAṬA ĀKAṬA MOHAYA MOHAYA AMUKĪM ĀKARṢAYA JAḤ SVĀHĀ.

Having powdered the fruit of the *kapittha* tree, one should saturate it seven times with buffalo curd. Placing that powder in fresh buttermilk contained within a new vessel, one should add a small amount of it; in a mere moment, it becomes curd.
Having ground a kapittha fruit, one should smear a new vessel with it; milk boiled therein becomes curd free from whey.
One should cause milk to boil in an unbaked jar. When curds have formed, one should break the jar with courage; thus the curds become a jar.
Having infused a new jar many times with the milk of the *arka* plant, the water poured into it appears like buttermilk.

On the tenth day after a woman’s first childbirth, one should take ashes and enter the water with two handfuls placed one above the other. Then, by means of the upper line, the water-jar dries up; by means of the lower line of ashes, it fills up.
On a Sunday, having uprooted *apāmārga* roots from the *sānicāmaula* [conjunction], one should fight while holding the two ends of separate sticks smeared with those roots against one's waist.

When a thick cloth is smeared with tin, lac, and *bālā* resin, it does not fall when water is poured upon it. Likewise, by climbing onto a cane mat smeared with that same substance, one does not sink in water.
Having ground earth-creeper and fireflies together with oil and rubbed them well, whatever is smeared with that substance glows at night.
Having formed a paste of *āmalakī* with salt in a copper vessel, one should apply it to an iron vessel so that it appears like copper.
When heated cow-dung is sprinkled with powdered realgar, it bursts into flame.
Having placed a small flower or similar object upon the seed of a *ṛṇṭaka* plant, it falls when water is poured over it.
Having thrown a bee into a hollowed-out sparrow’s nest within a bamboo thicket, one should release it into the sky; it then flies about.
A dried fish, when saturated with oil of *bhallātaka* and placed in water, moves about.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the Chapter on Curiosity, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekallavīra.
Chapter A22. Then the Blessed One said:
"Prāṇa is in the heart; apāna is in the anus; samāna is in the region of the navel."
Udāna is located in the region of the throat, while vyāna pervades the entire body.
Among these, this vital breath (prāṇavāyu) is the primary one, situated in the heart;
through its division into inhalation and exhalation, it constitutes the life of all living beings.
By means of each of the sixteen transits, there is one *daṇḍa*;
by the flow of the four maṇḍalas, there are sixteen hundred and two thousand [breaths].
The fire-maṇḍala is said to be that which carries the sensation of the right;
the wind-maṇḍala is said to be that which carries the sensation of the left.
From an equal touch on the left and right, the Maheśvara-maṇḍala arises;
this very same [touch], when intense and mild, becomes the Vāruṇa-maṇḍala.
Lalanā is the left channel, while rasanā is situated on the right;
avadhūtī is indeed in the middle region, and it flows during the moment of innate bliss (sahajānanda).
Upon the entry [of the breath] into its full expansion, there is creation; stability arises from its motionless state;
and destruction occurs when the breath has departed—this process continues as long as life lasts.
Entering [the breath] is to be known as *kumbhaka* (retention), and its holding is *pūraka* (inhalation);
exiting is to be known as *recaka* (exhalation), while that which is motionless is considered *stambhaka* (suspension).
Having stabilized Caṇḍaroṣa together with Prajñā, one should begin;
one should count the wind as it enters by numbers such as a hundred thousand and so forth.
It is accomplished at that very moment, just as the word of the Lord Buddha says:
for he who, embracing Wisdom intensely, should count the single wind.
Through the form of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa, one attains accomplishment in a mere fortnight;
endowed with divine knowledge, one indeed becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā).
Established in the Caṇḍaroṣa-samādhi, he should embrace his own consort firmly,
holding heart to heart and joining secret organ to secret organ.
Having joined mouth to mouth, motionless and intent on bliss,
one should visualize the moon within the heart together with the sun.
By the power of that very steadiness alone, a person shall become omniscient.
By the mere taking up of tranquility, one knows the past, the future, and the present, as well as the minds of others; I speak this as the truth.
Likewise, by that very yoga, one should visualize within the middle of the ear;
thus one hears every sound located in all places as if it were nearby.
Likewise, having empowered the eyes, one perceives the three worlds;
and likewise, having meditated upon the nose, one knows all fragrances.
And by meditating likewise upon the object of the tongue, a distant taste becomes known; and by meditating likewise upon the tip of one's own organ, one perceives every tactile sensation.
Having meditated thus in the center of the head, which increases all power,
Wherever the mind is made of one flavor with the breath, there it is restrained;
in that very place, it reflects itself.
Pacification, enrichment, subjugation, attraction, as well as killing,
and expulsion— all these indeed are accomplished through meditative cultivation alone.
Through the practice of breath-retention (kumbhaka) and other techniques, one should employ the four gazes.
The gaze that looks to the left shall bring [the object] under control by means of breath-retention.
She who attracts the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be known as joined with inhalation (pūraka);
however, that gaze which is fixed on the forehead is the "slayer" (māraṇī) when joined with exhalation (recaka).
Indeed, his gaze fixed on the tip [of the nose] cannot be diverted by one who performs the act of immobilization;
for retention (*kumbhaka*) is practiced upon the *parā* flower, and inhalation (*pūraka*) upon the *snuhī* plant.
Recaka should be practiced on a sap-filled tree, and Stambhaka on a swaying blade of grass;
indeed, one should contemplate [the object] for six months, employing the previously established gaze.
But one endowed with all powers succeeds through the restraint of the mind;
for by the restraint of the mind comes the restraint of the vital wind, and by the restraint of the vital wind [comes the restraint of the mind].
There would also be a mutual obstruction of the movement and activity of the mind;
however, when wisdom and means are joined as one in the union of the vajra and the lotus, [such obstruction does not occur].
For one who has ceased [ordinary perception] and enjoys bliss, the Lord of Lamentation is accomplished;
Vajrasattva and the other Buddhas are the companions of that mantra-practitioner.
Furthermore, why are the worldly gods such as Śaṅkara and others even mentioned?
For the Lord Tattvācala has been well-guarded by me in all the tantras.
Having performed worship for his sake, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who are like the sky and possess great supernatural powers, will appear.
Even the Buddhas of the present are indeed endowed with the wisdom of a Buddha;
therefore, the yogi should always and constantly contemplate the immovable Lord.
For one who does not know the Immovable, their birth in this world is fruitless;
indeed, without it, not even the slightest accomplishment can be attained.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, on the yoga of the winds, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekallavīra.
Chapter A23. Then the Blessed One said:

"By piercing the soles of the feet and piercing the navel, death shall occur within three nights. By piercing the soles of the feet and piercing the eyes, [death shall occur] within three months. By piercing the soles of the feet and piercing the nose, [death shall occur] within three months."

At the time of the hut-fire, [death occurs] with a thunderclap during the rains; from piercing the barber’s pit, in five years; when the tip of the tongue is no longer visible, in three days; from piercing the tip of the ear, in four months; from piercing the *ūrṇā* (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows), in one day; at the beginning or end of sexual intercourse, with a thunderclap after one month; and equally, from all minor piercings, in one month.

Through piercing the heart and throat simultaneously, [the result is attained] in three fortnights; through piercing the three palates simultaneously, in three days; through the ringing of a bell in the ears during sexual union, in three months; through piercing the base of the ear, the space between the eyebrows, and the crown of the head individually, in one day each; and through piercing from the big toe up to the navel, in six months.

From the loosening of the flesh at the tip of the nose, death occurs in seven nights; from the cutting of the flesh of the cheeks, in five months; from the non-appearance of tears from the eyes, in five months; from the crookedness of the nose, in seven days; from the depression of the heart, in a fortnight; from a drawn line in the middle of the tongue, in two nights; from the appearance of redness in the nails, in six months; and from the drying of the teeth, in six months.

From the non-appearance of the star Arundhatī, death occurs in six months; from the reversal of the seasons, such as cold occurring at the time of heat and so forth, and from seeing cracks everywhere, in one fortnight; from the sound "ha" due to cold and the sound "phuḥ" due to heat, in ten days; from seeing a drawn line at the base of the ring finger, in eighteen days; from not hearing the sound of the body being rubbed and from coldness in all limbs, in ten days; from the drying up of the heart and feet immediately after bathing, in two months; and from a foul odor of the limbs, in three nights.

From stiffness of the limbs, death occurs in one day; from urine flowing counter-clockwise, in six months; from the inversion of the navel, in five days; from the non-appearance of the tip of the nose, in five months; from the non-appearance of light when pressing the eyes or fingers, in ten days; from not hearing the sound in the ears, in a year; and from not seeing one's reflection in another's eye, in a fortnight.
Having understood this deception, one should contemplate the next world.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, on the characteristics of death, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra*, known as the *Ekallavīra*.
Chapter A24. Then the Blessed One said:
"From the union of mother and father, the moon consists of the five elements."
The sun consists of the five elements through the conjunction of the union of the two.
There, indeed, a being consisting of wisdom and means is born again;
from the moon comes the binding of the bones, and from the sun arises the flesh and so forth.
The body of sentient beings, fashioned by karma, is empty of a self;
its nature is like an illusion and like a city of the Gandharvas.
And this [body] is considered equal to Indra’s bow and like the moon reflected in water.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, on the nature of the body, in the *Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra* known as the *Ekallavīra*.
Chapter A25. Then the Blessed Lady said:
"I wish to hear further regarding the arising of the perfection of wisdom."
Grant me your favor, O Protector; [explain] it concisely, not too extensively.
Then the Blessed One said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the arising of the Perfection of Wisdom—
the Goddess who sits in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, possessing the form of a sixteen-year-old."
She is blue in color, highly fortunate, and sealed by Akṣobhya;
she holds a red lotus playfully in her right hand and [a water jar] in her left.
The Kāmaśāstra indeed stands [there], [depicting] her seated upon a lotus and moon,
with full and elevated breasts, proud, large-eyed, and sweet-spoken.
Abiding in the innate, immovable samādhi, one should meditate upon this goddess,
the yoginī Viśvavajrī, who is born from the gnosis of the syllable HŪṂ.
The yogi should meditate on her while embracing [the consort]; he will certainly attain accomplishment.
Alternatively, he should meditate on Śvetā, who arises from the syllable *dhīḥ*.
One should visualize Vajradhātvīśvarī, sealed by Śāśvata, yellow in color;
or Kurukullikā, red in color, sealed by Ratneśa and holding a lotus.
The goddess sealed by Amitābha, born from the wisdom of the syllable Hrīṃ;
or Tārā, green in color, born from the wisdom of the syllable Tāṃ.
A person should meditate upon Amoghamudrā in her former form,
seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture and abiding in a gentle appearance.
The glorious one, holding a sword and a noose, performing the gesture of embracing, and being skillful,
should take a maiden of his own family or another family and empower her.
By this, the yogi succeeds through the mudrā; of this there is no doubt.
Alternatively, having fashioned an image prepared from clay or other materials, he should accomplish [the practice].
Established in the innate fierce samādhi, one should recite with a one-pointed mind.

In this regard, the mantra to be recited is as follows: Oṃ vivajri āgaccha āgaccha hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajrasarasvatī āgaccha āgaccha dhīḥ svāhā | Oṃ vajradhātvīśvarī āgaccha āgaccha vaṃ svāhā | Oṃ kurukulle āgaccha āgaccha hrīṃ svāhā | Oṃ tāre āgaccha āgaccha tāṃ svāhā ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Ekavīra maṇḍala:
it is square, with four doors and adorned with four archways.
A four-petalled lotus of yellow color should be drawn in the center;
its eastern petal is white, and the one in the south-west is like blood-red.
In the northwest [direction] it is yellow in color, while in the northeast corner it is dark green;
in the center it is indeed black in color—one should thus fashion Acala there.
One should visualize [the deity] as standing upon the sun, white, yellow, red,
or dark blue, appearing as a single form through the five Buddhas.
And Locanā is in the southeast corner,
holding a moon and an *aśoka* flower in her left and right hands, with a radiance like the rays of the autumnal moon.
In the southwest is the supreme goddess Pāṇḍarā, bearing a bow and arrows;
in the northwest corner is Māmakī, who is red and resembles the color yellow.

In the northeast corner is the dark-complexioned Tāriṇī, who bestows boons; she holds a water-pot, grain, and a crest in her hands, and carries a blue lotus in her left hand while holding [the other implements] in her right.
All these [deities] have the moon as their seat and are seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).
One should place Rāgavajrī at the eastern gate, seated upon a throne made by Śakra.
She is red in color, holding a sword and a skull-bowl, and is Dveṣavajrā; she is blue, holding a flaying knife and a raised index finger, and has Yama as her seat.
In the west, one should place Mānavajrā, belonging to the family of the axe-vajra holder, wearing a peacock-feather garment and stationed upon Varuṇa.
All these [deities] are seated upon sun-discs, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, wrathful, and with their hair disheveled.
Indeed, four jars resembling yellow in color should be placed in the corners;
by the mere meditation upon this, one is endowed with the eight Yoginīs.
That Supreme Lord, the husband of women, resides throughout the three worlds.
Now I shall further explain another meditation on Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa:
one should visualize the deity Caṇḍaroṣaṇa within the center of a universal lotus;
Rāmadeva is in the southeast, while the red-colored one is in the southwest.
Kāmadeva is indeed yellow, while the one named Māhilla is dark;
in the northwest is the one known as Kokilāsura, who is black in color.
These [deities], holding a curved knife and a skull-bowl, stand in the *ālīḍha* posture;
behind the Blessed One stands the goddess Parṇaśāvarī.
By means of this very yoga of meditation and by worshipping the burnt fish and other [offerings], one should bind all the gods.
Caṇḍaroṣa is blue, joined with yellow Prajñā on his left, who holds a white lotus;
or else he is joined with red or black [Prajñā].
The yogi who has reached perfection in meditation attains success at that very moment;
in this way, one should meditate upon Śvetācala and the others with intense effort.
Even without a seed-syllable, one should meditate with a mind concentrated in one-pointedness—
whether drinking, eating, sleeping, standing, walking, or even while pacing.
A yogi, remaining in every state, should meditate on the form of the deity;
or else, he should meditate on pure bliss, rejoiced by the pair of Yoginīs.
One should contemplate intensely until clarity is attained;
once it has become perfectly clear, the yogi achieves accomplishment through the Mahāmudrā.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Sadhana of the Deity, in the Śrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra known as the Ekallavīra.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Śrī Vajrasattva; and those hosts of yogins and yoginīs rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.
Thus ends the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Tantra, titled the Ekallavīra.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
